content.text:
So Q10(a): On Sept 10, 2026, 5 CFR 330.602 definition of "displaced" paragraph (1) contained only the introductory text: "A current competitive service employee in the competitive service tenure group at grade GS-15 (or equivalent) or below (or another qualifying competitive service appointment, as determined by OPM) who:" — with no subparagraphs (i) and (ii), because the final rule's amendatory instruction 11 set out only the introductory text and thereby removed (1)(i) and (1)(ii). This made the definition incomplete (literally "who:" with nothing following).

(b) What changed: correction 2026-18800, published Sept 15, 2026, effective Sept 15, 2026, restored paragraphs (1)(i) and (1)(ii) as they read before the final rule. Why without notice and comment: good cause under 5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B), because it makes no substantive change—restores text in effect before Sept 2, 2026, that OPM did not propose to remove and the final rule did not discuss removing; and 553(d)(3) effective upon publication. How characterized: "no substantive change"; correcting amendment.

(c) After the change: paragraph (1)(i): "Received a RIF separation notice under part 351 and has not declined an offer under part 351, subpart G, of a position with the same type of work schedule and a representative rate at least as high as that of the position from which the employee will be separated."

So if Nadia is offered a full-time position with a lower representative rate than her present full-time position and declines: she has not declined an offer of a position with same type of work schedule and representative rate at least as high. The offer is lower, so declining it does not disqualify her—she is still "displaced" under (1)(i). What if same representative rate? Same type of work schedule (full-time) and representative rate at least as high -> she has declined such an offer -> she is not "displaced" under (1)(i).

Wait: "same type of work schedule and a representative rate at least as high as that of the position from which the employee will be separated." If position offered is full-time and her present is full-time, same schedule yes; representative rate lower -> not "at least as high" -> declining doesn't disqualify; still displaced. If same representative rate -> at least as high -> declined -> not displaced. Good.

Now Q1(d): Which RIFs governed by amended rules and which stay under earlier rules; where stated. DATES: 91 FR 49178: "This rule is effective September 2, 2026. An agency that issued a RIF notice before the effective date of the rule must process the RIF under the regulations in effect when the RIF notice was issued. An agency that issues a RIF notice on or after the effective date must apply the RIF provisions as amended by this final rule." Is there more detail in preamble "Implementation Considerations" lines 3395-3418? Let's read. Also Q1(e) need details on other rules: 2026-15666 (appeals) changes part 351: adds subpart I? effective Sept 2, in force today. 2026-21316 Managing Senior Professional Performance—what does it change in part 351? Need inspect. 2026-21320 Administrative leave—amends 351.806, effective Nov 18 (not yet in force today Nov 14). Q1(e) asks "with effect on or after the main rule's effective date. For each, give document number, what it changes in part 351, its effective date, and whether it is in force today." So:
- 2026-15666: effective 2026-09-02; in force today (Sept 2 < Nov 14). Changes part 351: adds new subpart I? Replaces MSPB appeal procedures with OPM; likely adds 351.901-351.910? Need read TOC.
- 2026-21316: effective 2026-11-18; not in force today; what does it change in part 351? Maybe amends 351.503(d)/(e) cross-reference? Let's inspect.
- 2026-21320: effective 2026-11-18; not in force today; amends 351.806 (administrative leave during notice period).
- 2026-13715 effective 2026-08-06, before Sept 2 -> not list. But maybe it amended 5 CFR 351.503 references? It's before main rule, so not "with effect on or after" main rule's effective date. Exclude, but maybe mention.

Also maybe 2026-21316 and 2026-21320 both published Oct 19. Check their CFR text.

Let me read the TOC for 2026-15666, 2026-21316, 2026-21320.

    60  [Docket ID: OPM-2025-0239]
    61  RIN 3206-AO99
    62  
    63  
    64  Reduction in Force Appeals
    65  
    66  AGENCY: Office of Personnel Management.
    67  
    68  ACTION: Final rule.
    69  
    70  -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    71  
    72  SUMMARY: The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) is issuing final 
    73  regulations to revise how an employee may appeal a furlough of more 
    74  than 30 days, separation, or demotion by a reduction-in-force (RIF) 
    75  action. OPM will replace the Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB) as 
    76  the adjudicative agency for such appeals. The rule establishes a 
    77  uniform, record-based OPM appeal process; clarifies the appellant's 
    78  burden; requires production of the complete agency record; preserves 
    79  collateral statutory remedies; and applies prospectively to improve 
    80  timeliness, consistency, and cost-effectiveness while maintaining 
    81  administrative review.
    82  
    83  DATES: Effective September 2, 2026. This final rule applies only to a 
    84  RIF action for which an agency issues the employee a specific RIF 
    85  notice under 5 CFR 351.802 on or after September 2, 2026.
    86  
    87  FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT: Aaron Gottesman, Senior Advisor to the 
    88  Director, by email at [email protected] or by phone at 
    89  (202) 606-7400.
    90  
    91  SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: OPM is issuing this final rule to modernize 
    92  the administrative process for appeals by employees who are furloughed 
    93  for more than 30 days, separated, or demoted by a reduction-in-force 
    94  action under 5 CFR part 351. Congress charged OPM with prescribing 
    95  regulations governing the release of competing employees in a RIF, and 
    96  OPM has historically implemented RIF appeal procedures through 
    97  regulation. This final rule revises that regulatory framework by 
    98  replacing the prior MSPB forum for future non-SES RIF appeals with a 
    99  uniform OPM-administered process. The rule does not alter agencies' 
   100  responsibility to determine their workforce needs or whether a RIF is 
   101  necessary. By requiring a complete RIF-specific agency record, 
   102  permitting an appellant reply, authorizing additional information, 
   103  audits, investigations, and hearings when necessary and efficient, and 
   104  preserving collateral statutory remedies, the final rule provides 
   105  meaningful administrative review while reducing delay, fragmentation, 
   106  and unnecessary litigation burden.
   107  
   108  I. Digest of Public Comments and Summary of Changes From the Proposed 
   109  Rule
   110  
   111      In response to the proposed rule, OPM received 1,252 comments 
   112  during the 30-day public comment period from a variety of individuals, 
   113  including current and former civil servants, members of Congress, as 
   114  well as organizations, including local and national unions and Federal 
   115  agencies. Of the 1,252 comments, 1,251 were posted on 
   116  www.regulations.gov, and one was not posted because it contained vulgar 
   117  language unrelated to the rulemaking in question. At the conclusion of 
   118  the public comment period, OPM reviewed and analyzed the comments. In 
   119  general, the comments ranged from ardent support of the proposed 
   120  regulation to categorical rejection of it. Less than 1 percent of the 
   121  overall comments were supportive, neutral, or mixed, and 99 percent 
   122  opposed the proposed regulation.
   123      OPM found many of the comments helpful. OPM has revised the final 
   124  rule to clarify, narrow, or supplement the proposed RIF appeal 
   125  procedures in response to comments, including comments concerning 
   126  burden of proof, access to the agency record, information asymmetry, 
   127  due process, neutrality, hearings, protective orders, collective 
   128  bargaining, and public disclosure. In response to those comments, the 
   129  final rule adds more precise appeal standards, a detailed RIF-specific 
   130  agency-record requirement, disclosure and privilege protections, 
   131  stronger adjudicator-separation and ex parte safeguards, narrower e-
   132  filing sanctions, more flexible reply rules, and more carefully 
   133  tailored protective order and public posting provisions. The revisions 
   134  are summarized below.
   135      Clarifying appealable actions. The final text clarifies the 
   136  appealable actions set forth in Sec.  351.901(a). The proposal allowed 
   137  an employee ``who has been the subject of a reduction-in-force action'' 
   138  to appeal an action taken under part 351. The final text specifies that 
   139  only an employee furloughed for more than 30 days, separated, or 
   140  demoted by a RIF action taken under part 351 may appeal that action to 
   141  OPM.
   142      Revising the merits standard. The final text replaces the proposed 
   143  ``would not have suffered the same or another RIF action'' standard in 
   144  Sec.  351.901(b) with a more precise two-part merits showing: the 
   145  appellant must prove that the agency failed to comply with an 
   146  applicable statute or OPM regulation governing RIF actions under part 
   147  351, and the failure prejudiced the appellant by causing the appealed 
   148  action or the loss of a materially more favorable outcome. This is 
   149  clearer and better focused on prejudicial RIF-compliance error.
   150      Revising exclusivity language. The final text continues to provide 
   151  that part 351 procedures are the sole and exclusive means of appealing 
   152  a RIF action, and adds that RIFs and matters related to the appeals of 
   153  RIFs cannot be raised in grievance procedures or challenged through 
   154  grievance arbitration, while expressly preserving collateral matters 
   155  within the independent jurisdiction of Equal Employment Opportunity 
   156  Commission (EEOC), Inspectors General, MSPB, Department of Labor 
   157  Veterans' Employment and Training Service (DOL VETS), and the Office of 
   158  Special Counsel (OSC). The final text also retains the no-judicial-
   159  review provision.
   160      Updating filing-system language. The final text replaces the 
   161  proposed placeholder for the electronic filing system with a reference 
   162  to the system identified on OPM's website. It also replaces 
   163  ``statements, evidence, or documents'' with ``pleadings, evidence, or 
   164  documents,'' better aligning the filing provision with adjudicatory 
   165  terminology.
   166      Clarifying filing deadlines. The final text changes the filing 
   167  deadline from 11:59 p.m. Eastern Standard Time to 11:59 p.m. Eastern 
   168  Time, avoiding confusion during daylight saving time. It also 
   169  consolidates the untimely-filing rule in Sec.  351.902(b)(2) and 
   170  provides that good-cause determinations are within OPM's sole and 
   171  exclusive discretion.
   172      Adding a limited tolling rule for collateral matters. The final 
   173  text adds Sec.  351.902(b)(3), which permits an employee who timely 
   174  filed a collateral matter within the independent jurisdiction of an 
   175  entity identified in Sec.  351.901(c) to file a RIF appeal within 30 
   176  calendar days after the final decision on that matter, where that 
   177  decision materially affects the employee's retention standing, order of 
   178  release, assignment rights, or other rights under part 351. The final 
   179  text provides that a decision is final for this purpose when it is no 
   180  longer subject to further administrative review and that OPM 
   181  determines, in its sole and exclusive discretion, whether the decision 
   182  materially affects the employee's rights.
   183      Requiring filing-information detail in the RIF notice. The final 
   184  text amends Sec.  351.802(a)(6) to require the specific RIF notice to 
   185  state, in addition to the employee's right to appeal to OPM, the
   186  
   187  [[Page 49231]]
   188  
   189  time limit for filing an appeal under Sec.  351.902(b) and the 
   190  electronic filing system through which an appeal must be filed.
   191      Narrowing e-filing enforcement. The final text narrows the proposed 
   192  e-filing enforcement provisions. Rather than authorizing broader orders 
   193  regulating filing methods, sanctions, misuse, or termination of e-filer 
   194  participation, the final text provides that OPM may strike a document 
   195  when an e-filer repeatedly fails to follow filing instructions after a 
   196  show-cause order. The final text also removes the proposed statement 
   197  that withdrawal from e-filing may preclude future re-registration and 
   198  clarifies that withdrawal of e-filing registration is not good cause 
   199  for staying a case.
   200      Simplifying initial-appeal information. The final text simplifies 
   201  the contact-information requirements in Sec.  351.903(a) by replacing 
   202  ``legal name, best address'' with ``name, address.'' The core 
   203  requirement remains unchanged: the appeal must be written, state the 
   204  basis for the appeal, identify the appellant and any representative, 
   205  and include supporting documentation.
   206      Defining the agency record. The final text adds a RIF-specific 
   207  minimum agency-record requirement to Sec.  351.903(b). The proposal 
   208  required the agency response to include the agency record but did not 
   209  define its contents. The final text specifies that the agency record 
   210  includes, at a minimum, the RIF notice and effective-date documents, 
   211  documents supporting the RIF reason, coverage and appointment records, 
   212  competitive-area and competitive-level records, retention-register and 
   213  retention-standing records, order-of-release records, assignment-rights 
   214  records, special RIF-circumstance records, and a certification that the 
   215  complete agency record has been produced.
   216      Distinguishing production to OPM from service on the appellant. The 
   217  final text requires the agency to produce the complete agency record to 
   218  OPM while serving the appellant with the agency record subject to 
   219  legally required limits. The agency may redact or withhold information 
   220  from the appellant's copy only to the extent necessary to comply with 
   221  the Privacy Act, applicable legal privileges, classified-information or 
   222  national-security requirements, OPM protective orders, or other 
   223  disclosure limits required by law.
   224      Allowing limited new matters in reply. The final text revises Sec.  
   225  351.903(c) to permit an appellant's reply to raise a new allegation of 
   226  error if the basis for that allegation rests on information first 
   227  disclosed in the agency response or if OPM grants leave for good cause.
   228      Adding disclosure limits for inspection and service. The final text 
   229  makes inspection of OPM's appellate record and service of documents 
   230  subject to the Privacy Act, applicable legal privileges, classified-
   231  information or national-security requirements, OPM protective orders, 
   232  and other applicable disclosure limits required by law. The proposal 
   233  allowed inspection and required service but did not include the same 
   234  express disclosure limitations.
   235      Reorganizing representative provisions. The final text reorganizes 
   236  Sec.  351.904 into separate paragraphs addressing designation of a 
   237  representative, Federal employee representatives and restrictions on 
   238  official time and reimbursement, and disallowance of representatives. 
   239  The final text also narrows the grounds for disallowing a 
   240  representative. Because a Federal employee representative may not 
   241  perform representational functions while in a duty status, the final 
   242  text does not adopt the proposed additional grounds for disallowance 
   243  based on the priority needs of the Government or unreasonable costs to 
   244  the Government; OPM or the responsible agency may disallow an 
   245  employee's choice of representative only where the representative is an 
   246  employee of the responsible agency or OPM and the representative's 
   247  activities would cause a conflict of interest or position. The 
   248  remaining changes are primarily organizational and clarifying.
   249      Adding adjudicator-separation and ex parte safeguards. The final 
   250  text adds safeguards in Sec.  351.905(a) requiring OPM adjudicators to 
   251  be insulated from officials who participated personally and 
   252  substantially in the challenged action or provided case-specific 
   253  advice. It also prohibits adjudicators from considering material ex 
   254  parte communications on the merits and requires any such communication 
   255  to be summarized in the record with an opportunity for party response, 
   256  unless disclosure is prohibited by law.
   257      Clarifying OPM employee appeals. The final text clarifies that an 
   258  administrative law judge (ALJ) assigned to adjudicate an OPM employee's 
   259  appeal will issue an initial decision. It also adds material factual 
   260  error affecting the outcome as a ground on which OPM may disturb the 
   261  ALJ's decision and clarifies that assigning an ALJ does not make 5 
   262  U.S.C. 554, 556, or 557 applicable unless independently required by law 
   263  or expressly incorporated.
   264      Tightening audits and investigations. The final text narrows the 
   265  standard for OPM audits or investigations. The proposal allowed OPM to 
   266  conduct an audit or investigation when the ``interest of justice'' 
   267  would be served. The final text requires OPM to determine that the 
   268  existing record is insufficient to resolve a material issue within 
   269  OPM's jurisdiction and that the audit or investigation is reasonably 
   270  likely to produce material information. The final text also provides 
   271  that representatives may not participate in an audit or investigation 
   272  unless OPM specifically requests it.
   273      Removing a separate ascertainment sanction. The final text removes 
   274  the proposed separate paragraph authorizing sanctions for failure to 
   275  participate in ascertainment of facts and renumbers the initial-
   276  decision and remedies provisions.
   277      Refining protective-order authority. The final text revises Sec.  
   278  351.906(a). The proposal focused on harassing communications and use of 
   279  appeal information for unrelated purposes. The final text authorizes 
   280  protective orders or cease-and-desist directives to protect the 
   281  integrity of the adjudicatory process and to prevent threats, 
   282  intimidation, targeted harassment, improper witness contact, disclosure 
   283  of protected personal information, or misuse of nonpublic information 
   284  obtained through the appeal. It also requires protective orders to be 
   285  no broader than reasonably necessary and not to restrict lawful 
   286  communications protected by law.
   287      Clarifying OPM-initiated reconsideration. The final text clarifies 
   288  in Sec.  351.907(a) that OPM may reopen and reconsider an initial 
   289  decision either upon request of a party or on its own initiative. The 
   290  proposal allowed party-requested reconsideration, while Director sua 
   291  sponte review was addressed separately.
   292      Clarifying Director review. The final text revises Sec.  351.908 to 
   293  preserve the Director's sua sponte authority to reopen and reconsider a 
   294  nonfinal initial decision or reopened and reconsidered decision, while 
   295  identifying nonexclusive considerations that may guide that review. The 
   296  proposal gave the Director broad discretion to reopen and reconsider 
   297  any nonfinal decision. The final text clarifies that the Director may 
   298  consider whether the decision contains clear legal error, rests on an 
   299  erroneous material factual finding, involves an issue of exceptional 
   300  importance, affects governmentwide civil service administration, 
   301  conflicts with another OPM decision, or otherwise warrants review. It 
   302  also clarifies that Sec.  351.908 does not create a party right to 
   303  request Director review and that, upon reopening, the Director may take 
   304  any action available under Sec.  351.907(c).
   305  
   306  [[Page 49232]]
   307  
   308      Revising finality of initial decisions. The final text revises 
   309  Sec.  351.909 so that an initial decision becomes final 30 calendar 
   310  days after issuance unless, before that time, a party timely requests 
   311  reopening and reconsideration under Sec.  351.907 or the Director 
   312  reopens the decision under Sec.  351.908. A timely request suspends 
   313  finality: if OPM denies or dismisses the request without reopening the 
   314  initial decision, the initial decision becomes final 30 calendar days 
   315  after issuance of the denial or dismissal unless the Director reopens 
   316  it before that time, and if OPM grants the request, the reopened and 
   317  reconsidered decision becomes final 30 calendar days after issuance 
   318  unless the Director reopens that decision before that time. An untimely 
   319  request does not suspend or otherwise affect finality. The final text 
   320  also clarifies that a decision by the Director that disposes of the 
   321  appeal is final and effective upon issuance and that, if the Director 
   322  remands the appeal or directs further proceedings, any resulting 
   323  decision becomes final under Sec.  351.909. These changes conform 
   324  finality to the reconsideration and Director-review provisions of the 
   325  final rule.
   326      Adding public-posting disclosure limits. The final text adds 
   327  express legal limits on public posting of final merits decisions, 
   328  including requirements protecting privacy, privileged information, 
   329  protected personnel information, law-enforcement-sensitive information, 
   330  and other information that may not lawfully be disclosed. It also 
   331  clarifies that final merits decisions not publicly posted because of 
   332  such legal limits must be made available upon request to the Federal 
   333  employee or former Federal employee involved in a proceeding under this 
   334  subpart, his or her representative selected pursuant to Sec.  351.904, 
   335  or a representative of the Federal agency or office involved in the 
   336  proceeding who has a need to know.
   337      OPM is finalizing the RIF appeals rule as amended. After 
   338  considering the comments, OPM concludes that the final rule, as 
   339  amended, better balances timely adjudication, governmentwide 
   340  consistency, employee access to meaningful administrative review, and 
   341  agencies' need for finality in workforce restructuring than the current 
   342  MSPB appeal process for non-SES RIFs.
   343  
   344  II. Background
   345  
   346      When agencies face workforce restructuring, RIF procedures provide 
   347  a mechanism for realigning staff through objective criteria. These 
   348  procedures are governed by 5 U.S.C. 3501-3504 and are implemented 
   349  through OPM regulations at 5 CFR 351. These regulations provided 
   350  employees subject to a RIF action with an avenue to appeal to the MSPB. 
   351  Under the previous 5 CFR 351.901, replaced by this rule, employees 
   352  furloughed for more than 30 days, separated, or demoted by a RIF action 
   353  were able to appeal to the MSPB.
   354      Federal RIF procedures govern the release of competing employees 
   355  when a release is required because of lack of work, shortage of funds, 
   356  insufficient personnel ceiling, reorganization, or the exercise of 
   357  reemployment or restoration rights. Congress has directed OPM to 
   358  prescribe regulations governing the release of competing employees in a 
   359  RIF, giving due effect to the statutory retention factors specified in 
[... continue with --start 360]

  4497  Sec.  351.905  Adjudication of appeals.
  4498  
  4499      (a) Appeals by non-OPM employees. OPM will assign personnel to 
  4500  adjudicate an appeal under this subpart by an employee of an agency 
  4501  other than OPM. OPM personnel assigned to adjudicate an appeal under 
  4502  this subpart shall be insulated from officials who participated 
  4503  personally and substantially in the challenged personnel action or 
  4504  provided case-specific advice concerning that action. OPM adjudicators 
  4505  shall not consider material ex parte communications concerning the 
  4506  merits of an appeal. If such a communication occurs, OPM will place a 
  4507  summary of the communication in the record and provide the parties a 
  4508  reasonable opportunity to respond, unless disclosure is prohibited by 
  4509  law. In addition, no OPM employee may be assigned to adjudicate an 
  4510  appeal if the employee has a relationship with the appellant or, during 
  4511  the preceding two years, that person was an employee of the agency that 
  4512  is a party to the action to be assigned, or the employee was subject to 
  4513  an action covered under this part. When necessary, OPM may assign an 
  4514  administrative law judge to preside over the adjudication of an appeal.
  4515      (b) Appeals by OPM employees. OPM will assign an administrative law 
  4516  judge to adjudicate an appeal under this subpart by an OPM employee and 
  4517  to issue an initial decision. To insulate the adjudication of its own 
  4518  employees' appeals from agency involvement, OPM will not disturb 
  4519  initial decisions in those cases unless a party shows that there has 
  4520  been harmful procedural irregularity in the proceedings before the 
  4521  administrative law judge, a clear error of law, or a material factual 
  4522  error that affected the outcome of the appeal. For the purposes of 
  4523  paragraph (b) of this section, the term harmful procedural irregularity 
  4524  means an irregularity in the application of procedures that was likely 
  4525  to have caused the administrative law judge to reach a conclusion 
  4526  different from the one he or she would have reached in the absence or 
  4527  cure of the irregularity. The assignment of an administrative law judge 
  4528  under paragraph (b) or under paragraph (a) of this section does not 
  4529  make 5 U.S.C. 554, 556, or 557 applicable to an appeal under this 
  4530  subpart except to the extent those provisions are independently 
  4531  required by law or expressly incorporated in this part.
  4532      (c) Ascertainment of facts. OPM may require either party to provide 
  4533  additional information, and it may audit or investigate an agency's 
  4534  action in the course of adjudicating an appeal if it determines, in its 
  4535  sole discretion, that the existing record is insufficient to resolve a 
  4536  material issue within OPM's jurisdiction, and that the audit or 
  4537  investigation is reasonably likely to produce information material to 
  4538  resolving that issue. An individual serving as a representative of 
  4539  either party may not participate in an audit or investigation unless 
  4540  OPM specifically requests them to do so. The review of an agency action 
  4541  must be based solely on the developed written record unless OPM 
  4542  determines that a hearing is
  4543  
  4544  [[Page 49266]]
  4545  
  4546  necessary and efficient in resolving an appeal. For purposes of this 
  4547  section, the phrase necessary and efficient means circumstances in 
  4548  which the written record is insufficiently developed to make a 
  4549  determination regarding one or more facts material to the outcome of

  4559      (d) Initial decision. OPM will notify the employee, employee's 
  4560  representative, and agency in writing of its decision.
  4561      (e) Remedies. (1) If the employee is the prevailing party, OPM will 
  4562  order relief including correction of the personnel action and any back

  4567      (2) If the agency timely requests reconsideration of an initial

content.text:
Great. Q7 answers:
(b) Morgan notice Oct 19, 2026; separation effective Friday Dec 18, 2026. Appeal to OPM; must file via OPM's electronic filing system identified on OPM's website (351.902(a)). Deadline: within 30 calendar days from effective date; first day counted is day after effective date; if last day falls Saturday, Sunday, Federal holiday, filing period includes first workday after. Effective date Dec 18, 2026. Count: day 1 = Dec 19. 30th day = Jan 17, 2027? Dec 19 + 29 days = Jan 17. Let's compute: Dec 19 to Dec 31 = 13 days (19,20,...,31). Jan 1-17 = 17 days; total 30. So 30th day = Sunday, Jan 17, 2027. Next: Jan 18, 2027 is MLK Day (Federal holiday). First workday after = Tuesday, Jan 19, 2027. Deadline 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time on Jan 19, 2027. Need to confirm Jan 17, 2027 is Sunday. 2027 Jan 1 is Friday? Let's check: 2026 Jan 1 is Thursday? 2024 leap year Jan 1 Monday; 2025 Jan 1 Wednesday; 2026 Jan 1 Thursday; 2027 Jan 1 Friday. So Jan 17, 2027 is Sunday (Jan 1 Fri, Jan 2 Sat, Jan 3 Sun; Jan 10 Sun; Jan 17 Sun). Yes. Jan 18 Monday = MLK Day (third Monday of January = Jan 18, 2027). So deadline Jan 19, 2027, 11:59 p.m. ET.

(c) What must she prove: by preponderance of evidence: timeliness; OPM jurisdiction; agency failed to comply with applicable statute or OPM regulation governing RIF actions; and failure prejudiced her by causing the appealed action or loss of materially more favorable outcome (351.901(b)). Hearing: not entitled as of right; review based solely on written record unless OPM determines a hearing is necessary and efficient (351.905(c)). So possible hearing within OPM discretion, not entitlement.

(d) Union challenge via negotiated grievance procedure: 351.901(c)(2): RIF action and any matter relating to appeal may not be raised under negotiated grievance procedure or contested through grievance arbitration. Preamble on collective bargaining (lines 1828-2027) says what about existing agreements? Need read. Likely says the rule applies notwithstanding existing CBAs; maybe not retroactive? Let's read that section.

(e) Judicial review: 351.901(c)(4): "A party cannot obtain judicial review of a decision under this subpart." Also 351.909(e): no further right of appeal. So no.

(f) OSC complaint filed before appeal deadline, final decision March 10, 2027 correcting rating, which would have changed retention standing. Can she still appeal RIF and by when? 351.902(b)(3): If before expiration of filing period, employee timely filed a complaint/appeal/other matter within independent jurisdiction of an entity in 351.901(c), and final decision materially affects retention standing, order of release, assignment rights, or other rights under part 351, employee may file an appeal within 30 calendar days after date decision becomes final and no longer subject to further administrative review. March 10, 2027 final decision -> 30 calendar days after = April 9, 2027. Need count: March 10 + 30 days: March 11 is day 1; March has 31 days, so March 11-31 = 21 days; April 1-9 = 9 days; total 30 -> April 9, 2027. What day? 2027 April 9 is Friday? Jan 1 Fri; Apr 1 Thursday (Jan 31 Sunday? let's compute later). Even if weekend, rule 351.902(b)(1) applies "if date ordinarily last day falls on Saturday, Sunday, or Federal holiday, filing period will include first workday after." April 9, 2027: Jan 1 Friday; Jan 31 Saturday? Jan 1 Fri, Jan 8 Fri, Jan 15 Fri, Jan 22 Fri, Jan 29 Fri; Jan 31 Sunday. Feb 1 Monday; Mar 1 Monday; Apr 1 Thursday. Apr 9 Friday. Yes April 9, 2027. Good. But Q asks "Can she still appeal the RIF, and by when?" Yes, under 351.902(b)(3), provided the OSC complaint was timely filed before expiration of the original filing period and the final decision materially affects rights. OPM determines in sole discretion whether material. Deadline 30 calendar days after final decision (March 10, 2027) -> April 9, 2027 (11:59 p.m. ET). But also: is a complaint to OSC within "entity identified in Sec. 351.901(c)"? Yes, Office of Special Counsel. Good.

(g) Which provision decides between (a) and (b)? Cite exactly where stated. The DATES section of 2026-15666 at 91 FR 49230: "This final rule applies only to a RIF action for which an agency issues the employee a specific RIF notice under 5 CFR 351.802 on or after September 2, 2026." Perhaps also 351.901? The "applicability" is in DATES. Q7(g) asks "Which provision decides between (a) and (b)? Cite exactly where it is stated." Likely the DATES statement. Maybe also MSPB rule's effective date clause. We'll cite DATES of 2026-15666 and 2026-16456 (which says Board will continue to adjudicate RIF appeals for actions before effective date). But the "provision" deciding between (a) notice Aug 31 vs (b) Oct 19 is the applicability sentence in DATES. Give FR page 49230.

Now Q7(a): Which body hears appeal for notice Aug 31, 2026 and separation Oct 30, 2026? Under OPM final rule, applies only to specific RIF notice issued on or after Sept 2, 2026. Notice Aug 31 -> not covered; prior rules (MSPB) apply. MSPB's Appellate Jurisdiction Update II (2026-16456) effective Sept 2, 2026: removes references to RIF appeals, but says "consistent with OPM's rulemakings, the MSPB will not apply this rule to pending cases or to newly filed cases relating to agency actions taken before the effective date of OPM's rulemakings, and will continue to adjudicate such probationary termination appeals, suitability appeals, and RIF appeals." So MSPB hears it. Also the OPM proposed rule (2026-02576) may state prospective application; the OPM final rule's DATES; the MSPB rule. Maybe also the OPM final rule correction? Doesn't bear. "Every 2026 document that bears on the answer": 2026-15666 (DATES), 2026-16456 (MSPB rule dates), perhaps 2026-02576 proposed (proposed prospective application), maybe 2026-17338 correction (no). Also there might be a law? no. Need to check MSPB rule text for exact statement. Read 2026-16456 fully (2 pages). Later.

Q7(d) preamble existing agreements: read lines 1828-2027 in appeals final rule. Also Q7(e) judicial review section 1579-1742 maybe for statements. Q7(f) collateral claims 1742-1828. Let's read those sections selectively. Also the preamble section on subpart I (2349-3032) will have preamble statements for Q14(i) and maybe discrepancies. Need to read.

Let's read 1579-2027 (judicial review, scope, collective bargaining).

[2026-15666: lines 1579-1978 of 4700, FR page 49242]
  1579  G. Judicial Review and CSRA Exclusivity
  1580  
  1581      Many commenters, including but not limited to 0033, 0046, 0114, 
  1582  0308, 0386, and others, criticized the proposed rule's foreclosure of 
  1583  judicial review for RIF appeals adjudicated under the amended 5 CFR 
  1584  part 351. Commenters 0033, 0908, and 1114 asserted that the APA 
  1585  requires OPM to maintain judicial review of RIF appeals, while 
  1586  Commenter 0343 argued that OPM barring judicial review would be an 
  1587  ultra vires action. Commenters 0370, 0928, 1025, 1089, 1092, 1099, and 
  1588  1165 argued that OPM cannot eliminate judicial review by regulation, 
  1589  that judicial review is constitutionally required, that APA review 
  1590  should remain available, and that Federal Circuit review of MSPB 
  1591  decisions has long served as an important external check on RIF 
  1592  adjudication.
  1593      OPM disagrees that the final rule eliminates judicial review that 
  1594  Congress provided. The prior Federal Circuit review path for non-SES 
  1595  RIF appeals depended on two things: OPM's regulation making RIF actions 
  1596  appealable to MSPB and the statutory provisions governing judicial 
  1597  review of MSPB decisions. Once OPM revises its regulation and no longer 
  1598  provides MSPB as the forum for non-SES RIF appeals, the MSPB-to-
  1599  Federal-Circuit review path no longer applies.
  1600      Congress did not provide a separate statutory judicial-review route 
  1601  for non-SES RIF appeals under 5 U.S.C. 3502. The CSRA and related title 
  1602  5 provisions establish a comprehensive remedial scheme for Federal 
  1603  personnel matters, ``prescrib[ing] in great detail the protections and 
  1604  remedies applicable to such action[s], including the availability of 
  1605  judicial review.'' Fausto, 484 U.S. at 443; see also Margolin v. Nat'l 
  1606  Ass'n of Immigr. Judges, No. 25-767, slip op. at 1-3 (U.S. May 26, 
  1607  2026) (Thomas, J., concurring). Where Congress provides review, it does 
  1608  so expressly. Where Congress does not provide a judicial-review route 
  1609  for a particular personnel matter, employees may not use the APA to 
  1610  create an alternative route for challenging that personnel action. See 
  1611  Filebark v. U.S. Dep't of Transp., 555 F.3d 1009 (D.C. Cir. 2009), 
  1612  cert. denied, 558 U.S. 1007 (2009); Fornaro v. James, 416 F.3d 63, 66-
  1613  67 (D.C. Cir. 2005); Graham v. Ashcroft, 358 F.3d 931, 933-35 (D.C. 
  1614  Cir. 2004); Carducci v. Regan, 714 F.2d 171, 172 (D.C. Cir. 1983).
  1615      The CSRA prescribes in precise detail the types of actions that 
  1616  result in eventual judicial review, and it does not provide for such 
  1617  review of non-SES RIFs. 5 U.S.C. 3595(c). Under the CSRA, ``[t]he 
  1618  reviewable agency actions are removal, suspension for more than 14 
  1619  days, reduction in grade or pay, or furlough for 30 days or less.'' 
  1620  Elgin v. Dep't of the Treasury, 567 U.S. 1, 5-6 (2012). Courts have 
  1621  repeatedly dismissed actions brought outside the proper CSRA channels 
  1622  (such as under the APA) by individuals regarding their employment under 
  1623  the comprehensive statutory scheme provided for in the CSRA. See, e.g., 
  1624  Bush v. Lucas, 462 U.S. 367, 368 (1983); Zummer v. Sallet, 37 F.4th 996 
  1625  (5th Cir. 2022); Dotson v. Griesa, 398 F.3d 156, 163 (2d Cir. 2005).
  1626      What is given by the comprehensive statutory scheme in the way of 
  1627  RIF procedures are codified at 5 U.S.C. 3501-3504. While those statutes 
  1628  technically predate the CSRA's enactment in 1978, it has long been 
  1629  recognized that the statutes and regulations regarding reductions-in-
  1630  force in the Federal Government are part of the ``comprehensive 
  1631  employment scheme'' created by the CSRA.\21\ While RIF separations can 
  1632  result in job loss or reassignment, they are specifically excluded as 
  1633  adverse actions under Chapter 75 of Title 5, U.S. Code, which governs 
  1634  removals and discipline for misconduct and, in some cases, performance 
  1635  deficiencies. See 5 U.S.C. 7512(B) (``This subchapter . . . does not 
  1636  apply to . . . a reduction in force action under [Sec.  ] 3502 of this 
  1637  title.'').
  1638  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1639  
  1640      \21\ Filebark v. U.S. Dep't of Transp., 555 F.3d 1009, 1010 
  1641  (Fed. Cir. 2009); see also Nat'l Treasury Emps. Union v. Vought, 149 
  1642  F.4th 762, 774-75 (D.C. Cir. 2025) (applying CSRA claims-channeling 
  1643  in a lawsuit challenging, inter alia, reductions in force); Nat'l 
  1644  Treasury Emps. Union v. Trump, 770 F. Supp. 3d 1, 11 (D.D.C. 2025) 
  1645  (same); Gober v. Collins, No. 25-cv-714 (RC), 2025 WL 1360434, at *6 
  1646  (D.D.C. May 8, 2025) (same).
  1647  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1648  
  1649      ``A RIF is an administrative procedure by which agencies eliminate 
  1650  jobs and account for employees who occupied abolished positions. It is 
  1651  not an adverse action against a particular employee, but it is directed 
  1652  solely at a position within an agency.'' Huber v. Merit Systems 
  1653  Protection Bd., 793 F.2d 284, 286 (Fed. Cir. 1986). ``Unlike adverse 
  1654  actions, RIFs are not aimed at removing particular individuals; rather 
  1655  they are directed solely at positions.'' Grier v. Dep't of Health & 
  1656  Human Servs., 750 F.2d 944, 945 (Fed. Cir. 1984). MSPB concurs, noting 
  1657  the Board's authority ``is not plenary,'' but rather ``the scope of the 
  1658  Board's jurisdiction to review an agency's RIF actions [are] under 
  1659  OPM's regulations at 5 CFR part 351,'' which do not implement Chapter 
  1660  75. Adams v. Dep't of Defense, 96 M.S.P.R. 325, 329 (2004).
  1661      The final rule therefore provides that a party cannot obtain 
  1662  judicial review of a decision under part 351. That provision governs 
  1663  decisions issued under the regulatory RIF appeal process established by 
  1664  this rule. It does not displace collateral statutory claims that 
  1665  Congress has assigned to other forums or that carry their own review 
  1666  provisions. Final Sec.  351.901(c) expressly preserves matters within 
  1667  the jurisdiction of the EEOC, Inspectors General, MSPB where it has 
  1668  independent jurisdiction, DOL VETS, and OSC.
  1669      OPM also disagrees that due process requires Article III review of 
  1670  every RIF appeal. A RIF is a position-based workforce action governed 
  1671  by part 351, not a disciplinary or performance-based adverse action 
  1672  under chapter 75. The final rule preserves notice, a written appeal, 
  1673  production of the agency record, service on the appellant subject only 
  1674  to legally required disclosure limits, a reply, inspection of OPM's 
  1675  appellate record, additional fact development where warranted, hearings 
  1676  when necessary and efficient, written decisions, reconsideration, and 
  1677  corrective relief. OPM concludes that these procedures provide 
  1678  meaningful administrative review for the regulatory RIF appeal right 
  1679  established under part 351.
  1680      Commenters 0033 and 0846 argue that Congress has not spoken clearly 
  1681  on judicial review of RIF appeals. OPM disagrees. The statutory scheme 
  1682  speaks through both text and structure.
  1683  
  1684  [[Page 49243]]
  1685  
  1686  Congress expressly excluded ``a reduction-in-force action under section 
  1687  3502'' from the chapter 75 adverse-action provisions, 5 U.S.C. 7512(B), 
  1688  and the chapter 75 MSPB appeal right applies only to actions covered by 
  1689  that subchapter. See 5 U.S.C. 7513(d). Chapter 77 likewise does not 
  1690  independently create a statutory RIF appeal right; it provides 
  1691  procedures for matters otherwise ``appealable to the Board under any 
  1692  law, rule, or regulation.'' 5 U.S.C. 7701(a). Judicial review under 5 
  1693  U.S.C. 7703(a)(1), in turn, attaches to a ``final order or decision'' 
  1694  of MSPB. Once OPM withdraws the regulatory delegation that made non-SES 
  1695  RIF actions appealable to MSPB, there is no MSPB decision for judicial 
  1696  review under section 7703. Commenters identify no provision in 5 U.S.C. 
  1697  3501 through 3504, chapter 75, chapter 77, or any other Federal 
  1698  employment statute that creates judicial review for non-SES RIF appeals 
  1699  under section 3502. The omission is significant. As the Supreme Court 
  1700  explained in Fausto, Congress's failure to provide review in the CSRA 
  1701  is not a statutory accident but reflects ``a considered congressional 
  1702  judgment.'' 484 U.S. at 448. Congress also demonstrated that it knows 
  1703  how to provide MSPB review of RIF-related actions when it chooses to do 
  1704  so, as it did for certain SES RIF actions. See 5 U.S.C. 3595(c). It did 
  1705  not enact comparable language for non-SES RIF actions under section 
  1706  3502. This omission is significant. It is a basic canon of statutory 
  1707  construction that if ``Congress includes particular language in one 
  1708  section of a statute but omits it in another section of the same Act, 
  1709  it is generally presumed that Congress acts intentionally and purposely 
  1710  in the disparate inclusion or exclusion.'' \22\
  1711  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1712  
  1713      \22\ INS v. Cardoza-Fonseca, 480 U.S. 421, 432 (1987).
  1714  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1715  
  1716      Commenter 0343 argued that OPM cannot preclude judicial review by 
  1717  regulation. The final rule does not withdraw judicial review that 
  1718  Congress provided; it reflects the review scheme Congress enacted. The 
  1719  prior route to Federal Circuit review existed only because OPM's 
  1720  regulation made non-SES RIF actions appealable to MSPB, and section 
  1721  7703 then provided review of final MSPB decisions. OPM may revise that 
  1722  regulatory delegation through notice-and-comment rulemaking. Nor does 
  1723  the APA supply an independent route around the CSRA. The APA does not 
  1724  apply where ``statutes preclude judicial review,'' 5 U.S.C. 701(a)(1), 
  1725  and courts have repeatedly held that the CSRA is the exclusive remedial 
  1726  scheme for Federal personnel disputes, even where the CSRA provides 
  1727  limited or no relief.\23\ Accordingly, there is no statutory basis for 
  1728  extending judicial review to OPM decisions in non-SES RIF appeals under 
  1729  part 351. OPM's regulations stating that judicial review of RIF actions 
  1730  is unavailable informs the public of the operative legal parameters. 
  1731  Judicial review would be equally unavailable if the final rule said 
  1732  nothing on the subject.
  1733  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1734  
  1735      \23\ See Elgin v. Dep't of Treasury, 567 U.S. 1, 11-12 (2012); 
  1736  Grosdidier v. Chair. of Broad. Bd. of Governors, 560 F.3d 495, 497 
  1737  (D.C. Cir. 2009); Filebark v. Dep't of Transp., 555 F.3d 1009, 1010 
  1738  (D.C. Cir. 2009); Graham v. Ashcroft, 358 F.3d 931, 935 (D.C. Cir. 
  1739  2004); Fornaro v. James, 416 F.3d 63, 67 (D.C. Cir. 2005).
  1740  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1741  
  1742  H. Scope of RIF Appeals and Collateral Claims
  1743  
  1744      Commenters 0370, 0928, 0962, 1025, 1089, 1092, 1099, 1165, and 1217 
  1745  raised concerns about the scope of OPM review and the preservation of 
  1746  collateral claims. Commenters argued that the proposal could weaken 
  1747  civil-rights enforcement, eliminate mixed-case processing, prevent 
  1748  employees from raising pretext or retaliation, or force employees into 
  1749  multiple forums. Commenters 0046, 0074, 0540, and 1252 contended that 
  1750  the rule would eliminate the ability to appeal discrimination claims in 
  1751  connection with RIFs entirely and allow agencies to RIF employees in 
  1752  protected classes with impunity.
  1753      The final rule clarifies the scope of OPM's review. OPM will 
  1754  adjudicate whether the agency failed to comply with an applicable 
  1755  statute or OPM regulation governing RIF actions under part 351 and 
  1756  whether that failure prejudiced the appellant. This includes RIF-
  1757  compliance issues such as coverage, competitive area, competitive 
  1758  level, retention standing, order of release, assignment rights, notice, 
  1759  special RIF circumstances, and related requirements.
  1760      At the same time, the final rule preserves collateral statutory 
  1761  avenues. Final Sec.  351.901(c) states that the procedures in part 351 
  1762  are the sole and exclusive means of appealing a RIF action, but do not 
  1763  otherwise preclude an employee from filing a complaint, appeal, or 
  1764  other matter within the jurisdiction of EEOC, an Inspector General, 
  1765  MSPB, DOL VETS, or OSC. This provision reflects OPM's intent to channel 
  1766  direct challenges to RIF compliance through OPM while preserving 
  1767  matters Congress or applicable law has assigned to other forums.
  1768      OPM acknowledges that some claims previously could have been 
  1769  combined with a RIF appeal before MSPB because OPM's regulation made 
  1770  RIF actions appealable to MSPB. That prior combined forum was a 
  1771  consequence of OPM's regulatory delegation to MSPB, not an independent 
  1772  statutory requirement that OPM retain MSPB jurisdiction. The final rule 
  1773  preserves the substantive availability of discrimination, 
  1774  whistleblower, veterans' rights, prohibited-personnel-practice, and 
  1775  Inspector General matters in the proper forums.
  1776      Commenter 0463 asserted that the exclusive RIF appeal procedure 
  1777  could abrogate or supersede appeal rights available to preference 
  1778  eligible veterans under 5 U.S.C. 3330a and 3330b. OPM disagrees. The 
  1779  final rule's exclusivity provision governs direct appeals of RIF 
  1780  actions under part 351; it does not displace independent statutory 
  1781  causes of action that Congress assigned to other forums. Final Sec.  
  1782  351.901(c) expressly preserves an employee's ability to file a 
  1783  complaint, appeal, or other matter within the jurisdiction of, among 
  1784  others, MSPB and the Department of Labor Veterans' Employment and 
  1785  Training Service. That preservation language includes claims under the 
  1786  Veterans Employment Opportunities Act. Under 5 U.S.C. 3330a, a 
  1787  preference eligible who alleges that an agency violated the 
  1788  individual's rights under a statute or regulation relating to veterans' 
  1789  preference may file a complaint with the Secretary of Labor, and, if 
  1790  the matter is not resolved, may appeal to MSPB under the procedures 
  1791  Congress specified. 5 U.S.C. 3330a. Section 3330b separately provides 
  1792  for judicial redress in district court in lieu of continuing the 
  1793  administrative redress procedure after the statutory prerequisites are 
  1794  met. 5 U.S.C. 3330b. Nothing in this final rule alters those statutory 
  1795  rights, filing deadlines, forum assignments, or judicial-redress 
  1796  provisions.
  1797      The final rule also reinforces, rather than weakens, the ability to 
  1798  identify and address veterans' preference issues in a RIF appeal. 
  1799  Section 351.903(b) requires the agency record to include documents 
  1800  establishing the appellant's veterans' preference status and related 
  1801  retention information, including records supporting veterans' 
  1802  preference credit, tenure subgroup, service computation date, the 
  1803  retention register, order of release, assignment rights, and any 
  1804  special RIF circumstance relevant to the appellant. Thus, where the 
  1805  issue is whether the agency complied with part 351's RIF requirements 
  1806  as applied to a preference eligible, OPM will have the relevant RIF 
  1807  record before it. Where the issue is an independent veterans' 
  1808  preference claim under 5 U.S.C. 3330a
  1809  
  1810  [[Page 49244]]
  1811  
  1812  or 3330b, the final rule leaves that statutory route undisturbed.
  1813      Commenter 0074 similarly asserted that the revised RIF appeal 
  1814  procedure would allow agencies to engage in pretextual terminations of 
  1815  employees with disabilities in violation of the Rehabilitation Act of 
  1816  1973. OPM disagrees. The final rule does not authorize agencies to use 
  1817  RIF procedures as a pretext for disability discrimination or any other 
  1818  unlawful personnel practice. Federal employees and applicants remain 
  1819  protected by section 501 of the Rehabilitation Act, 29 U.S.C. 791, and 
  1820  the remedies, procedures, and rights available under 29 U.S.C. 794a, 
  1821  including the Federal-sector procedures incorporated from Title VII. In 
  1822  addition, disability discrimination remains a prohibited personnel 
  1823  practice under 5 U.S.C. 2302(b)(1)(D). The final rule expressly 
  1824  preserves matters within the jurisdiction of the EEOC and OSC and 
  1825  therefore does not redirect Rehabilitation Act claims into OPM's RIF 
  1826  appeal process or limit the remedies available under those statutes.
  1827  
  1828  I. Collective Bargaining, Grievance Arbitration, and CBAs
  1829  
  1830      Commenters 0962, 1025, 1092, 0928, and 1217 objected to the 
  1831  proposal's treatment of negotiated grievance procedures, arbitration, 
  1832  and collective bargaining agreements. These commenters argued that the 
  1833  Federal Service Labor-Management Relations Statute protects negotiated 
  1834  grievance and arbitration procedures; that RIF matters are not among 
  1835  the matters excluded from negotiated grievance procedures under 5 
  1836  U.S.C. 7121(c); that questions of arbitrability should be resolved 
  1837  through negotiated grievance procedures; and that OPM may not use a 
  1838  governmentwide regulation to eliminate existing collective-bargaining 
  1839  rights or union representation. Other commenters, including 0221, 0584, 
  1840  0587, 0591, and 0621, asserted that the proposal would unlawfully 
  1841  supersede existing CBAs, while commenters 0386 and 1004 requested a 
  1842  clearer legal basis for OPM's position. Commenters 0049, 0092, 0483, 
  1843  and others objected as a policy matter to any prospective limitation on 
  1844  negotiated RIF appeal procedures.
  1845      OPM has considered these comments and has decided to finalize the 
  1846  regulatory text as initially proposed, with some modifications. The 
  1847  final Sec.  351.901(c) provides that the procedures in part 351 are the 
  1848  ``sole and exclusive means'' of appealing a RIF action, and matters 
  1849  relating to such actions may not be raised under a negotiated grievance 
  1850  procedure or contested through grievance arbitration, but employees are 
  1851  not otherwise impeded from filing a complaint, appeal, or other matter 
  1852  within the jurisdiction of the EEOC, an Inspector General, MSPB, DOL 
  1853  VETS, or OSC.
  1854      OPM continues to conclude that a single governmentwide process for 
  1855  direct RIF-compliance appeals is necessary to ensure uniform 
  1856  interpretation and application of part 351. RIF appeals under part 351 
  1857  involve governmentwide rules governing competitive areas, competitive 
  1858  levels, retention standing, order of release, assignment rights, 
  1859  notice, and related requirements. Allowing agencies to create or 
  1860  bargain for parallel direct appeal mechanisms for the same RIF-
  1861  compliance claim would undermine the consistency, finality, and 
  1862  efficiency the final rule is designed to achieve.
  1863      This conclusion is consistent with 5 U.S.C. 7117(a)(1). That 
  1864  provision states that the duty to bargain extends only ``to the extent 
  1865  not inconsistent with any Federal law or any governmentwide rule or 
  1866  regulation,'' and, for matters that are the subject of a rule or 
  1867  regulation, applies only where the rule or regulation is not 
  1868  governmentwide. 5 U.S.C. 7117(a)(1). This final rule is a 
  1869  governmentwide regulation: it applies across agencies to appeals of 
  1870  covered RIF actions under part 351. To that end, it firmly and 
  1871  completely limits the flexibility of agencies to provide processes not 
  1872  contemplated by this rule, including grievance arbitration. See U.S. 
  1873  Dep't of Treasury, I.R.S. v. FLRA, 996 F.2d 1246, 1250 (D.C. Cir. 1993) 
  1874  (IRS) (5 U.S.C. 7117(a)(1) ``permits the government to pull a subject 
  1875  out of the bargaining process by issuing a governmentwide rule that 
  1876  creates a regime inconsistent with bargaining,'' including where a 
  1877  regulation ``sets out an exclusive method of resolving any claims''). 
  1878  Accordingly, agencies may not bargain for a claims-channeling process 
  1879  that conflicts with the final rule's designation of part 351 as the 
  1880  sole and exclusive means of directly appealing a RIF action.
  1881      OPM is not persuaded by commenters' argument that 5 U.S.C. 
  1882  7121(a)(1) overrides this conclusion. Section 7121(a)(1) requires CBAs 
  1883  to provide procedures for settlement of grievances, including questions 
  1884  of arbitrability, and makes those procedures the exclusive 
  1885  administrative procedures for grievances that fall within their 
  1886  coverage. But that provision must be read together with section 
  1887  7117(a)(1), which limits the duty to bargain where the matter is 
  1888  inconsistent with Federal law or a governmentwide rule or regulation. 
  1889  The broad definition of ``grievance'' in 5 U.S.C. 7103(a)(9) likewise 
  1890  does not displace section 7117(a)(1). The fact that RIFs are not listed 
  1891  in section 7121(c) does not mean parties may bargain for an alternative 
  1892  direct RIF appeal procedure that conflicts with a governmentwide 
  1893  regulation establishing a single appeal process.
  1894      The D.C. Circuit Court of Appeal's decision in IRS addressed 
  1895  exactly this issue. The court held that a union proposal that would 
  1896  permit grievances over contracting out was non-negotiable as it 
  1897  conflicted with OMB Circular A-76, a government-wide rule that 
  1898  prescribed the exclusive method for resolving disputes over contracting 
  1899  decisions. The court thus held that Circular A-76 prohibited bargaining 
  1900  over conflicting appeals processes. The final Sec.  351.901(c) 
  1901  similarly prohibits creating an alternative RIF appeals process through 
  1902  collective bargaining.
  1903      OPM also disagrees with Commenter 0962's assertion that section 
  1904  7121(a)(1) has primacy over section 7117(a)(1). Sections 7103, 7117, 
  1905  and 7121 are part of the same statutory scheme and must be read 
  1906  together. Section 7121 establishes negotiated grievance procedures for 
  1907  matters properly within a CBA's coverage; section 7117(a)(1) defines 
  1908  the outer boundary of the bargaining obligation where Federal law or a 
  1909  governmentwide regulation has occupied the field. Reading section 7121 
  1910  to require negotiated grievance arbitration of direct RIF appeals 
  1911  notwithstanding section 7117 would effectively nullify section 
  1912  7117(a)(1) for any matter that could be characterized as a grievance. 
  1913  In IRS the D.C. Circuit expressly rejected that statutory construction. 
  1914  OPM accordingly declines to adopt that reading.
  1915      Nor is this final rule merely a restatement of management rights 
  1916  under 5 U.S.C. 7106. Section 7106 preserves agency authority, subject 
  1917  to subsection (b), to determine mission, budget, organization, number 
  1918  of employees, internal security practices, and to lay off and retain 
  1919  employees, while also preserving bargaining over procedures and 
  1920  appropriate arrangements in appropriate circumstances. 5 U.S.C. 
  1921  7106(a), (b). The final rule does not simply repeat those management 
  1922  rights. It establishes a detailed governmentwide appellate process 
  1923  governing who may appeal, the burden of proof, filing deadlines, 
  1924  agency-record production, service, replies, inspection of the appellate 
  1925  record, representation, adjudication, protective orders, 
  1926  reconsideration, Director review, and finality.
  1927  
  1928  [[Page 49245]]
  1929  
  1930      For that reason, commenters' reliance on Office of Personnel 
  1931  Management v. FLRA, 864 F.2d 165 (D.C. Cir. 1988), is misplaced. In 
  1932  that case, the court addressed whether a governmentwide regulation that 
  1933  merely restated management rights could displace bargaining 
  1934  obligations. This rule does not merely restate a management right; it 
  1935  creates a specific, comprehensive appeal procedure for covered RIF 
  1936  actions. The final rule is therefore more closely aligned with the 
  1937  principle that a governmentwide rule may establish an exclusive method 
  1938  for resolving a particular category of claims, rather than simply 
  1939  invoking management rights at a high level of generality.
  1940      OPM also considered comments invoking the general purposes of the 
  1941  FSLMRS, including 5 U.S.C. 7101(a)(1), which recognizes that collective 
  1942  bargaining safeguards the public interest, contributes to the effective 
  1943  conduct of public business, and facilitates amicable dispute 
  1944  resolution. OPM does not dispute those principles. But section 7101 
  1945  must be read with the rest of chapter 71, including section 7117(a)(1), 
  1946  and with section 7101(b)'s direction that chapter 71 be interpreted 
  1947  consistently with the requirements of an effective and efficient 
  1948  Government. Those provisions support, rather than preclude, a 
  1949  governmentwide rule establishing one uniform process for direct RIF-
  1950  compliance appeals and prohibiting grievances over matters pertaining 
  1951  to RIF appeals.
  1952      In addition to the benefits of maintaining a uniform process for 
  1953  direct RIF-compliance appeals, OPM believes it is beneficial to 
  1954  foreclose grievance arbitration in particular as a forum for 
  1955  adjudicating RIF appeals. As OPM explained in the proposed rule, the 
  1956  arbitrators who adjudicate Federal-sector grievances are private 
  1957  contractors who typically do not have a background in agency operations 
  1958  or Federal employment law. This makes them ill-suited to evaluate 
  1959  potentially complex issues involved in arbitration appeals. OPM is 
  1960  aware of multiple studies showing that, across multiple 
  1961  administrations, the FLRA overturns arbitral awards at a high rate.\24\ 
  1962  The author of one of these studies, himself an arbitrator, concluded 
  1963  that ``Federal sector arbitration is more complex than private sector 
  1964  arbitration. The federal field is full of land mines in the form of 
  1965  laws with which federal sector arbitrators may be less familiar.'' \25\ 
  1966  Foreclosing grievance arbitration ensures adjudication will be handled 
  1967  by MSAC employees with specialized legal and subject matter expertise 
  1968  who are less likely to make reversible errors.
  1969  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1970  
  1971      \24\ See James Sherk, ``Federal Union Arbitrators Frequently 
  1972  Misapply the Law,'' (Aug. 2, 2023), https://www.americafirstpolicy.com/issues/expert-insight-federal-union-arbitrators-frequently-misapply-the-law (finding that between 2019 
  1973  and 2023 over 40 percent of arbitration awards were overturned or 
  1974  remanded upon appeal); see also Helburn, B. (2019). The Trump FLRA: 
  1975  Fair or foul (Helburn), at 6. https://cdn.govexec.com/media/gbc/docs/pdfs_edit/060619ew1.pdf (finding the FLRA set aside or remanded 
  1976  arbitration awards 80, 50, and 43 percent of the time in a sampling 
  1977  of cases arising under the Trump 45, Obama, and George W. Bush 
  1978  Administrations, respectively).

Excellent: Q7(d) answer: Rule 351.901(c)(2) prohibits raising RIF action or appeal matters under negotiated grievance procedure or grievance arbitration. Preamble: final rule does not retroactively invalidate existing CBAs or adjudicate particular CBA disputes; "OPM does not adopt" position that proposal would automatically vitiate existing agreements mid-term; when agreements renegotiated, governmentwide rule will limit duty/ability to bargain for inconsistent direct RIF appeal process; questions about particular existing agreement provisions, negotiability disputes, ULPs remain for chapter 71 forum. Cite 91 FR 49245.

Now Q7(f): tolling rule is 351.902(b)(3). Preamble summary says added. Good.

  2291  Because this final rule transfers adjudication of covered RIF appeals 
  2292  from MSPB to OPM, revised Sec.  351.802(a)(6) replaces the MSPB 
  2293  reference with a reference to OPM.
  2294      The revised provision requires an agency's RIF notice to inform the 
  2295  employee, as applicable, of the employee's right to appeal to OPM. As 
  2296  revised in this final rule, the notice must also state the time limit 
  2297  for filing an appeal under Sec.  351.902(b) and identify the electronic 
  2298  filing system, available on OPM's website, through which an appeal must 
  2299  be filed. This requirement preserves the practical filing information 
  2300  previously conveyed through the cross-reference to Sec.  1201.21 of 
  2301  this title and forecloses any contention that a RIF notice failed to 
  2302  apprise an employee of how and when to appeal. The provision is 
  2303  conforming in nature and is intended to ensure that employees receive 
  2304  accurate notice of the administrative appeal forum established by 
  2305  revised subpart I. The revision does not eliminate any independently 
  2306  applicable statutory notice requirement or any separately available 
  2307  remedial process administered by another entity.
  2308      The proposed rule retained legacy language in Sec.  351.802(a)(6) 
  2309  requiring agencies to comply with Sec.  1201.21 of this title, as 
  2310  applicable. OPM is removing that cross-reference in the final rule. 
  2311  Section 1201.21 is an MSPB notice provision that applies when an agency 
  2312  issues a decision notice in a matter appealable to the Board. It 
  2313  requires MSPB-specific information, including notice of the time limits 
  2314  for appealing to the Board, the address of the appropriate Board 
  2315  office, access to the Board's regulations, and access to the MSPB 
  2316  appeal form. Because this final rule replaces MSPB with OPM as the 
  2317  adjudicative forum for RIF appeals under part 351, retaining an 
  2318  unqualified cross-reference to Sec.  1201.21 in the RIF notice 
  2319  provision could create confusion about where an affected employee must 
  2320  file a RIF appeal.
  2321  
  2322  [[Page 49248]]
  2323  
  2324      This deletion is conforming, clarifying, and nonsubstantive. It 
  2325  does not eliminate any appeal right, shorten any filing period, alter 
  2326  the information an agency must provide about the OPM RIF appeal right, 
  2327  or affect any matter that remains independently appealable to MSPB. 
  2328  Rather, it removes an obsolete MSPB-specific notice cross-reference 
  2329  from a provision that now concerns OPM RIF appeals. To the extent an 
  2330  employee has an independent statutory or regulatory right to proceed 
  2331  before MSPB on a collateral matter, that right remains governed by the 
  2332  statutes and regulations applicable to that matter consistent with 
  2333  Sec.  351.901(c).
  2334  
  2335  B. Section 351.807--Certification of Expected Separation
  2336  
  2337      OPM is revising Sec.  351.807(e), which concerns agency 
  2338  determinations of eligibility for certification of expected separation. 
  2339  The prior provision referred to appeal to MSPB. Revised Sec.  
  2340  351.807(e) removes that MSPB reference and states that an agency 
  2341  determination of eligibility for certification may not be appealed.
  2342      This change is also conforming in nature. It aligns Sec.  
  2343  351.807(e) with revised subpart I and clarifies that certification 
  2344  determinations under Sec.  351.807 are not independently appealable 
  2345  under part 351. Employees who are actually furloughed for more than 30 
  2346  days, separated, or demoted by RIF action may pursue any appeal 
  2347  available under revised Sec.  351.901.
  2348  
  2349  C. Subpart I--Appeals
  2350  
  2351      OPM is revising subpart I of part 351 in full. Revised subpart I 
  2352  establishes the procedures governing appeals to OPM by employees who 
  2353  are subject to covered RIF actions. The revised subpart identifies who 
  2354  may appeal, the burden of proof, filing requirements, party 
  2355  submissions, representation rules, adjudication procedures, remedies, 
  2356  sanctions, reconsideration, Director review, and finality.
  2357  1. Section 351.901--Right To Appeal
  2358      Revised Sec.  351.901 establishes the right to appeal a covered 
  2359  reduction-in-force action to OPM, identifies the appellant's burden of 
  2360  proof, and defines the relationship between the OPM RIF appeal process 
  2361  and other remedial forums.
  2362      Paragraph (a) provides that an employee who has been furloughed for 
  2363  more than 30 days, separated, or demoted by a reduction-in-force action 
  2364  taken under part 351 may appeal that action to OPM. This paragraph 
  2365  identifies the covered actions that may be appealed under subpart I and 
  2366  implements the rule's central procedural change: OPM, rather than MSPB, 
  2367  will adjudicate appeals of covered RIF actions, subject to the 
  2368  applicability provision described below.
  2369      Paragraph (b) establishes the employee's burden of proof. The 
  2370  appellant must prove, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the 
  2371  written appeal was timely and in the required form; that OPM has 
  2372  jurisdiction over the appeal; that the agency failed to comply with an 
  2373  applicable statute or OPM regulation governing reduction-in-force 
  2374  actions under part 351; and that the failure prejudiced the appellant.
  2375      Paragraph (b)(4) defines the prejudice requirement. The appellant 
  2376  must show that the agency's failure to comply with an applicable RIF 
  2377  statute or OPM regulation caused the appellant to be subjected to the 
  2378  appealed action or to lose a materially more favorable outcome under 
  2379  part 351. This standard is intended to distinguish prejudicial errors 
  2380  from technical or immaterial errors. OPM will not grant relief solely 
  2381  because an agency committed a procedural or technical error if the 
  2382  appellant would have been subject to the same action, or would not have 
  2383  received a materially more favorable outcome, had the agency complied 
  2384  with the applicable requirement. Conversely, prejudice may exist where 
  2385  the violation affected the appellant's retention standing, order of 
  2386  release, assignment rights, notice rights, or other RIF determination 
  2387  in a way that materially affected the outcome of the RIF action as 
  2388  applied to the appellant.
  2389      Paragraph (c)(1) provides that the procedures in part 351 are the 
  2390  sole and exclusive means of appealing a RIF action covered by this 
  2391  subpart. This provision is intended to avoid duplicative or overlapping 
  2392  RIF appeal processes and to channel covered RIF appeals through the OPM 
  2393  procedure established by this final rule. It also promotes consistent 
  2394  application of OPM's governmentwide RIF regulations and avoids parallel 
  2395  adjudication of the same RIF-compliance issues in multiple forums.
  2396      Paragraph (c)(2) provides that a reduction-in-force action taken 
  2397  under part 351, and any matter relating to an appeal of such an action, 
  2398  may not be raised under a negotiated grievance procedure or contested 
  2399  through grievance arbitration. This provision forecloses negotiated 
  2400  grievance procedures and grievance arbitration as alternative forums 
  2401  for direct RIF-compliance challenges, for the reasons discussed in 
  2402  Section III.I of this preamble.
  2403      At the same time, paragraph (c)(3) makes clear that the OPM RIF 
  2404  appeal process does not displace matters within the independent 
  2405  jurisdiction of other entities. Employees may continue to file 
  2406  complaints, appeals, or other matters that fall within the independent 
  2407  jurisdiction of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, an 
  2408  Inspector General, MSPB, the Department of Labor Veterans' Employment 
  2409  and Training Service, or the Office of Special Counsel. Thus, OPM will 
  2410  adjudicate whether the RIF action complied with applicable RIF statutes 
  2411  and OPM regulations, while collateral statutory claims remain available 
  2412  in the forums Congress or applicable law has designated for those 
  2413  claims.
  2414      Paragraph (c)(4) also provides that a party cannot obtain judicial 
  2415  review of a decision under this subpart. OPM addresses comments 
  2416  concerning judicial review and the CSRA remedial scheme in Section 
  2417  III.G.
  2418      Consistent with the DATES section of this preamble, the appeal 
  2419  process established by revised Sec.  351.901 and subpart I is available 
  2420  for a reduction-in-force action for which the agency issued the 
  2421  employee a specific RIF notice under Sec.  351.802 on or after the 
  2422  effective date of the final rule under RIN 3206-AO86. An appeal of a 
  2423  reduction-in-force action for which the agency issued that notice 
  2424  before that date--including an appeal pending before the MSPB--
  2425  continues to be adjudicated by the MSPB under the procedures applicable 
  2426  when the action was taken. This applicability provision is stated in 
  2427  the preamble, and the final regulatory text accordingly does not 
  2428  include a separate applicability note in Sec.  351.901.
  2429  2. Section 351.902--Procedures for Submitting Appeals
  2430      Revised Sec.  351.902 describes the procedures and timeline an 
  2431  employee must adhere to when submitting an appeal.
  2432      Paragraph (a) requires a party, or the party's authorized 
  2433  representative, to file an initial appeal or request for 
  2434  reconsideration through the electronic filing system identified on 
  2435  OPM's website. Unless a party demonstrates good cause and obtains 
  2436  approval from OPM, OPM will not accept pleadings, evidence, or 
  2437  documents submitted by electronic mail or postal mail. This requirement 
  2438  is intended to promote consistent intake, reliable service, accurate 
  2439  case tracking, and efficient adjudication.
  2440      Commenters 0066, 0272, 0296, 0299, 0304, and others, criticized the 
  2441  requirement that employees use e-filing exclusively, absent a showing 
  2442  of good
  2443  
  2444  [[Page 49249]]
  2445  
  2446  cause. OPM disagrees with these criticisms. The good cause requirement 
  2447  permits nonelectronic filing methods for filers with a bona fide need 
  2448  while furthering OPM's legitimate interest in maintaining a streamlined 
  2449  case intake system that minimizes errors and delays. OPM notes that the 
  2450  e-filing requirement for RIF appeals for which this rule provides is 
  2451  consistent with the National Labor Relations Board's policy for 
  2452  requiring parties to e-file documents absent justification to file in 
  2453  paper format.\31\ Other agencies, including the FLRA and OSC, also have 
  2454  adopted restrictions on electronic filing.\32\ OPM acknowledges 
  2455  Commenter 0553's concern that the e-filing system described in the 
  2456  proposed rule was not operational and available for public inspection 
  2457  at the time the proposed rule was submitted for public comment. 
  2458  However, OPM is confident that it will have an e-filing system in place 
  2459  by this final rule's effective date.

  2461

  2463  permitted under this section, all documents filed in cases before 
  2464  the [National Labor Relations Board] must be filed electronically,'' 
  2465  and requiring paper filers to include ``a statement explaining why 
  2466  the party does not have access to the means for filing 
  2467  electronically or why filing electronically would impose an undue 
  2468  burden'').
  2469      \32\ See, e.g., 5 CFR 2429.24 (``To file documents by personal 
  2470  delivery, you must schedule an appointment at least one business day
