   241  leave for DRP programs prospectively, subject to the limits described 
   242  above. OPM agrees that Congress remains free to enact additional 
   243  workforce-transition authorities but disagrees that such legislation is 
   244  a prerequisite to the uses identified in this rule. The sponsors of the 
   245  Administrative Leave Act were concerned about costs associated with 
   246  open-ended investigations of employees and did not consider a use of 
   247  administrative leave that would produce long-term cost savings by 
   248  facilitating workforce reductions.
   249      OPM declines to withdraw the rule or to make changes based on this 
   250  line of comments. The final rule is a lawful exercise of OPM's 
   251  authority under 5 U.S.C. 6329a(c)(1), strengthens the regulatory 
   252  framework by converting policy guidance into binding prohibitions and 
   253  clarifying acceptable uses, preserves the duty-status presumption 
   254  during RIF notice periods, and does not alter the statutory 10-workday 
   255  limit or the investigative- and notice-leave framework of section 
   256  6329b.
   257  
   258  B. Cost of Administrative Leave and DRP
   259  
   260      Several comments, including 0004, 0016, 0022, and 0025, objected to 
   261  the cost of using administrative leave in conjunction with a DRP. 
   262  Comment 0004 stated the 2025 deferred resignation programs showed 
   263  waste, including paying employees who performed no work and later 
   264  rehiring. The commenter believes a full accounting of the DRPs should 
   265  be conducted before similar programs are codified in regulation. 
   266  Comment 0016 noted that the 2025 DRP placed tens of thousands of 
   267  employees in paid non-duty status for months while delivering no work 
   268  to the public, a direct payroll expenditure for zero output, compounded 
   269  by the loss of institutional knowledge, the collapse of continuity in 
   270  mission-critical functions, and the documented degradation of agency 
   271  capacity that followed. Comment 0022 commented that the proposed rule 
   272  attempts to justify the administration's costly workforce reduction 
   273  efforts, including widespread use of administrative leave, by promising 
   274  ``large long-term savings'' without providing concrete support or 
   275  considering downstream effects of letting employees participate in DRP.
   276      Comment 0022 also stated that OPM failed to provide concrete 
   277  support that justifies costly workforce reduction efforts, even as it 
   278  acknowledges the costs of the workforce reduction initiatives that 
   279  began in early 2025. The organization cited two recent studies that 
   280  highlight significant expenses tied to these workforce reduction 
   281  programs: (1) a June 2026 study estimated that deferred resignation 
   282  programs alone have cost at least $11 billion; and (2) another analysis 
   283  from April 2026 found that the Government paid approximately $4.5 
   284  billion in salary and benefits to employees who were not working under 
   285  DRP agreements.
   286      OPM respectfully disagrees with the commenters on the costs 
   287  associated with the original DRP. OPM acknowledged in the proposed rule 
   288  that there is a temporary cost to providing administrative leave and 
   289  stated its judgment that use of administrative leave in connection with 
   290  deferred resignation programs and other workforce restructuring 
   291  initiatives can generate long-term savings by reducing Federal staffing 
   292  levels. OPM did not project costs or savings from the proposed 
   293  regulations themselves because the regulations codify Governmentwide 
   294  policies already in place, and OPM does not expect codification to 
   295  produce significant changes in the usage of administrative leave.
   296      Further, OPM policy guidance has stated that use of administrative 
   297  leave in connection with DRP is in the interest of the agency and of 
   298  the Government as a whole because it facilitates workforce 
   299  restructuring and realignment efforts leading to a leaner, less 
   300  expensive, less wasteful, more efficient, and more mission-focused 
   301  Federal workforce. OPM also notes that this policy is not open-ended: 
   302  beginning in calendar year 2026, use of administrative leave by an 
   303  employee in connection with a workforce realignment initiative is 
   304  limited to 12 weeks in any individual instance unless a higher 
   305  threshold has been jointly approved by OPM and the Office of Management 
   306  and Budget. In addition, Sec.  630.1403(a)(6) requires an authorized 
   307  agency official to consider the effect on productivity and mission 
   308  needs and the strength of the justification for using appropriated 
   309  funds.
   310      OPM calculates that DRP separations in 2025 represented a workforce 
   311  reduction of over 6 percent, which contributed to the overall reduction 
   312  of the Federal workforce of over 12 percent from December 2024 to March 
   313  2026. Those workforce reductions create significant long-term savings 
   314  even after accounting for the one-time costs of DRP administrative 
   315  leave, which represent less than 3 percent of total basic payroll for 
   316  Federal employees. Because the payroll savings from a smaller workforce 
   317  recur in every subsequent fiscal year while the administrative leave 
   318  outlays are one-time transition costs, the long-term savings 
   319  substantially exceed the short-term costs even under the commenters' 
   320  own estimates.
   321      OPM makes no changes in the regulations in response to this line of 
   322  comments.
   323  
   324  C. 10-Workday Limit
   325  
   326      Comment 0025 asserted that the proposed rule exceeds OPM's 
   327  authority under the Administrative Leave Act of 2016, 5 U.S.C. 6329a-
   328  6329c, by establishing a regulatory exception to the statutory 10-
   329  workday calendar year limit. The commenter argued that the section 
   330  6329a(b) 10-workday calendar-
   331  
   332  [[Page 65927]]
   333  
   334  year limit reflects Congress's intent to curb extended agency-directed 
   335  paid non-duty status, that OPM's authority under section 6329a(c)(1) to 
   336  prescribe acceptable uses does not include authority to override that 
   337  limit, and that authorizing months of administrative leave for 
   338  workforce realignment, RIF notice periods, and settlements would render 
   339  the statutory cap ``optional and meaningless.'' The commenter urged OPM 
   340  to withdraw the proposal and seek legislation for any broader paid 
   341  transition or severance program. Similarly, comment 0029 asserted that 
   342  the proposed rule conflicts with the 10-workday limit Congress enacted 
   343  in section 6329a(b)(1) by ``re-authorizing exactly the indefinite, 
   344  uncontestable leave status Congress acted to eliminate.''
   345      However, comment 0029 supported retaining the language found in 
   346  proposed Sec.  630.1403(b)(3) concerning the use of administrative 
   347  leave for investigative purposes. A labor organization (0030) similarly 
   348  argued that the text and structure of the Act--including the separately 
   349  defined and expressly limited investigative leave authority in 5 U.S.C. 
   350  6329b--show that Congress withheld the power to provide unlimited 
   351  amounts of administrative leave, and cited the sense-of-Congress 
   352  findings accompanying the Act (5 U.S.C. 6329a note) that agency use of 
   353  administrative leave had exceeded reasonable amounts and that 
   354  administrative leave should be used sparingly.
   355      OPM disagrees that the rule exceeds its statutory authority. 
   356  Congress expressly directed OPM to ``prescribe regulations to carry 
   357  out'' section 6329a, including regulations governing the ``acceptable 
   358  agency uses of administrative leave'' and the recording of such leave 
   359  (5 U.S.C. 6329a(c)(1)). The final rule is an exercise of precisely that 
   360  delegated authority: it identifies acceptable and prohibited uses of 
   361  administrative leave and codifies existing Governmentwide policies to 
   362  promote consistency and accountability across agencies.
   363      The final rule does not waive, extend, or otherwise modify the 10-
   364  workday limit in section 6329a(b)(1). As OPM explained in the December 
   365  2024 final rule (89 FR 102256), the statutory limit applies where an 
   366  agency ``place[s]'' an employee on administrative leave for 
   367  investigative purposes. The 10-workday limit directly connects to a 
   368  provision in the investigative leave law (section 6329b(b)(3)(A)), 
   369  which bars placing an employee on investigative leave until the 10-
   370  workday limit is reached.
   371      The final rule preserves and indeed strengthens the statutory 
   372  framework. New Sec.  630.1403(b)(3) provides clarity by expressly 
   373  prohibiting use of administrative leave for investigative purposes once 
   374  the employee has reached the 10-workday limit. If necessary, an agency 
   375  may then use investigative leave under section 6329b, with all of that 
   376  section's procedural safeguards, approvals, time limits, and reporting 
   377  requirements. Thus, the final rule gives fuller effect to the statutory 
   378  scheme Congress designed for the specific problem that motivated the 
   379  Administrative Leave Act--prolonged, agency-directed removal of 
   380  employees from the workplace during personnel investigations.
   381      The commenter's reading--under which the 10-workday limit would 
   382  govern all extended uses of administrative leave--is inconsistent with 
   383  the position the commenter itself acknowledges: that general 
   384  administrative leave for purposes such as voting, blood donation, and 
   385  emergency closures remains outside the cap. The statute does not 
   386  enumerate acceptable purposes; it delegates that task to OPM. Nothing 
   387  in the text of section 6329a confines OPM's authority under subsection 
   388  (c)(1) to brief or de minimis uses, and the enumerated examples in 
   389  Sec.  630.1403(c) operate within, not around, the statutory limits: 
   390  uses that fall within the investigative context remain subject to the 
   391  10-workday limit, which when reached triggers coverage under section 
   392  6329b, while the workforce-realignment uses in paragraphs (c)(9) 
   393  through (c)(11) address categorically different circumstances, 
   394  discussed further below. The December 17, 2024, final rule cited by the 
   395  commenter included this sentence: ``An incidence of administrative 
   396  leave lasting more than 1 workday may be approved when determined to be 
   397  appropriate by an agency'' (5 CFR 630.1403(a)(3)). This final rule 
   398  simply adds specific examples of appropriate uses of administrative 
   399  leave for periods of more than 1 workday.
   400      The rule does not authorize unlimited administrative leave: the 
   401  workforce-realignment uses in Sec.  630.1403(c)(9) and (c)(11) are 
   402  expressly subject to Governmentwide limits established by OPM--
   403  currently 12 weeks in any individual instance absent joint OPM and 
   404  Office of Management and Budget approval of a higher threshold--and to 
   405  any agency limits, and every use of administrative leave remains 
   406  subject to the principles and decision factors in Sec.  630.1403(a).
   407      Finally, the ``Sense of Congress'' accompanying the Act--that 
   408  agencies should use administrative leave ``sparingly'' and manage its 
   409  costs prudently--is a non-binding statement of policy that informs, but 
   410  does not displace, the operative statutory text. The final rule is 
   411  consistent with that policy: it retains the general principles in Sec.  
   412  630.1403(a) that administrative leave is discretionary, should be 
   413  limited to the amount reasonably necessary, and ordinarily should not 
   414  exceed one workday for a single incidence, while identifying the 
   415  limited circumstances in which longer periods are appropriate. It also 
   416  adds new binding prohibitions (Sec.  630.1403(b)(3)-(5)) that constrain 
   417  agency use of administrative leave. As noted above, the sponsors of the 
   418  Administrative Leave Act were concerned about costs associated with 
   419  open-ended investigations of employees and did not consider a use of 
   420  administrative leave that would produce long-term cost savings by 
   421  facilitating workforce reductions.
   422      OPM makes no changes in response to these comments.
   423  
   424  D. Mission Capacity
   425  
   426      Three individual commenters (comments 0007, 0008, 0009) raised 
   427  concerns about the consequences of workforce reductions on the delivery 
   428  of Federal services. Comment 0007 described the impact of workforce 
   429  reductions on various public health services, communications during 
   430  emergencies, and technical assistance to states, and argued that the 
   431  proposed rule facilitates those reductions without accounting for their 
   432  effect on the public. Comment 0008 noted OPM's analysis should evaluate 
   433  the cost of reduced program capacity, including reduced preparedness 
   434  and loss of scientific expertise, rather than treating the cost of 
   435  administrative leave in isolation. Comment 0009 was concerned about the 
   436  loss of institutional and technical expertise, especially in 
   437  specialized topics and areas of work and requested that OPM clarify 
   438  that administrative leave is not to be used as a tool for permanent 
   439  downsizing and should not be used as a routine workforce reduction

content.text: Q8(b): "Under the adopted text and its companion leave provision, is employee consent needed, and is there a limit on how long this leave may last?" The companion leave provision is 630.1403(c)(10). It doesn't mention consent. 351.806(b) says agency may "place" employee on administrative leave — no consent. The 2026-21320 preamble says "'Provide' is a neutral term that accurately describes the provision of administrative leave with or without the employee's consent" (lines 1128-1136). As to limit: 12 weeks in any individual instance for workforce realignment initiatives? Wait, that 12-week limit mentioned at lines 301-305: "beginning in calendar year 2026, use of administrative leave by an employee in connection with a workforce realignment initiative is limited to 12 weeks in any individual instance unless..." Is that a Governmentwide limit established by OPM policy, not regulation. Does it apply to RIF notice period? It says workforce realignment initiative. 630.1403(c)(9) and (c)(11) are "subject to Governmentwide limits established by OPM"; (c)(10) (RIF) is not expressly subject. But the 12-week policy may apply to "workforce realignment initiative" broadly. Need read proposed rule or final preamble for statement that RIF administrative leave is subject to 12-week limit. Search "12 weeks" in doc.

So 12-week limit applies to "workforce realignment initiative" — does a RIF notice period count? Possibly yes, but 630.1403(c)(10) does not expressly incorporate Governmentwide limits. Q8(b) "Under the adopted text and its companion leave provision, is employee consent needed, and is there a limit on how long this leave may last?" Could answer: no consent required; 351.806(b) and 630.1403(c)(10) contain no durational cap, but leave must be consistent with subpart N; OPM policy's 12-week limit applies to "workforce realignment initiative" (perhaps including RIF), and 630.1403(a)(3) says usually not more than 1 workday, longer if appropriate. Need be careful and flag uncertainty.

But Q8(c): "What does OPM say allowed administrative leave during a RIF notice period before the adopted text takes effect?" likely answer: OPM policy guidance (CPM 2025-12, section D.1.b) already provided that an authorized agency official may provide administrative leave between receipt of a notice of involuntary separation and effective date of separation (lines 219-227). And under 5 U.S.C. 6329a(c)(1) / 5 CFR part 630 subpart N, agencies could use administrative leave; the rule codifies existing guidance. So Q8(c): OPM says its policy guidance allowed it—specifically section D.1.b of the Agency Policy Template (CPM 2025-12, July 30, 2025). Not the regulation itself. Good.

Now Q8(d): Does being on administrative leave change retention standing, notice rights or appeal rights? The preamble says new Sec. 630.1403(c)(10) and revised 351.806 address only paid non-duty status; do not alter substantive/procedural RIF requirements, including RIF competition, retention registers, appeal rights (lines 230-236). Also 351.806(a)/(b) no effect on 351.507 retention standing; notice rights under 351.801/802; appeal rights under 351.901. Answer: No. Cite preamble 91 FR 65926 and relevant provisions.

Now Q1(e): 2026-21316 changes to part 351: revises definition of "Rating of record" in 351.203 to include summary levels under 430.505(a)(6) for senior professionals; and 351.503(a)(1) adds "or the summary performance levels in Sec. 430.505(a)(6)" and revises (b)(2)/(3) to include part 430 subpart E. Effective Nov 18, 2026; not in force today (Nov 14). Good.

2026-21320 effective Nov 18; not in force today; amends 351.806 (status during notice period) and authority citation. In force today? No (effective Nov 18). Q1(e) asks "whether it is in force today." Today Nov 14. So 2026-15666 yes; 2026-21316 no; 2026-21320 no.

Need verify 2026-15666 is in force today: effective Sept 2, 2026, yes.

Any other final rule in 2026 amending part 351 with effect on or after Sept 2? Let's check cfr search 5:351 results: 7 docs. Excluding main final rule, corrections, 2026-13715 (effective Aug 6), leaves 2026-15666, 2026-21316, 2026-21320. Could there be a rule that amends part 351 but cfr affected field omits 351? E.g., "Elimination of Time-in-Grade" maybe amends 300; no. "Streamlining Probationary..." maybe 315/351? Search by query "part 351" in 2026 final rules. Let's do a keyword search for "5 CFR part 351" or "part 351" in rules published 2026.

content.text:
Compare proposed vs final as I read. Differences so far:
- 351.202(c)(3) proposed had typo "where such the reclassification"; final has "where the reclassification". (not real? typographical)
- 351.202(d) heading: proposed "Employees excluded. The provisions of this part do not apply to the following categories of employees:" final "Employees excluded from reduction in force competition. An employee holding one of the following appointments is not a 'competing employee'..." Substantive restructure. Proposed (d)(2)(iii): "temporary or term appointment of 1 year or less under subpart C or D of part 316"; final: "temporary appointment of one (1) year or less under subpart D of part 316." This is a real difference: proposed included term appointments and subpart C; final only temporary under subpart D. Also proposed (d)(3) allowed retain/furlough/separate/demote/reassign "without regard to the provisions of this part"; final (d)(3) more detailed and (d)(4) notice requirement added (final adds notice under 351.801 with specified content). This may be a Q11 difference.
- 351.203: proposed "Furlough ... not exceeding 1 year; but it does not refer ... and is instead dependent entirely on congressional action, rather than agency action." Final omitted that clause. Real difference? yes.
- Proposed "Initial probationary period ... described in Sec. 11.2 of this chapter and does not include ... described in subpart I of part 315" final "described in Sec. 11.2 of this part" (corrected later to chapter). Not substantive.
- Proposed "Rating of record ... pattern (as specified in Sec. 430.208(d)) of this chapter." Final "(as specified in Sec. 430.208(e))". Real? Citation difference? It's a substantive reference to pattern provision; change from (d) to (e). Could count as citation format? No, different paragraph. But Q11 says "a change in which section, subpart or part a cross-reference points to is not citation format." So this counts! Proposed 430.208(d) vs final 430.208(e).
- Proposed 351.204 only responsibility to follow; final adds "and for ensuring that such regulations are administered and applied consistent with all applicable laws, including the merit system principles set forth in 5 U.S.C. 2301(b)." Real difference.
- Proposed 351.301: "Removing the words 'competitive area' wherever they appear"; final "Removing the words 'competitive area' and adding ... 'agency'". Also proposed (b) removes parenthetical with text "i.e., in the gaining competitive area..."; final "removing the parenthetical phrase." Similar.
- Proposed 351.302(d): "use the adverse action procedures found in part 752 of this chapter"; final adds "or other procedures required by law, regulation, or the terms of the employee's appointment". Real difference.
- 351.402: proposed only revised paragraph (b); final revises paragraphs (b) and (c). Final adds new (c) 90-day OPM approval. Proposed didn't have (c) revision. But note proposed may have existing (c) unchanged. Real difference: final adds (c). Also final (b)(1) same. So Q11 difference.
- 351.501 same.
- 351.502: proposed uses "as of the date the agency issues a specific reduction in force notice" in several places; final uses "as of the date the employee receives a specific reduction in force notice." Real difference! Q5(c) asks event: which version of rules applies; end of four-year period; employee's tenure subgroup and retention standing. Under final, tenure subgroup as of date employee receives specific notice (351.502), whereas proposed used date agency issues notice. The final rule changed to receipt. Also 351.507 maybe. This is a key Q11 difference.

Continue reading proposed 351.502-351.507.

tools.name: fr_search

content.text:
Differences noted:
- 351.502: proposed uses "date the agency issues a specific reduction in force notice" vs final "date the employee receives a specific reduction in force notice." Multiple paragraphs. Real.
- 351.502(a)(3): proposed "not serving an initial probationary period or a temporary or time-limited appointment of 1 year or less under subpart C or D of part 316"; final "not serving an initial probationary period or a temporary appointment of 1 year or less under subpart D of part 316." Real.
- 351.502(b)(3) proposed typo "employees in the occupying"; final "employees occupying". Typo.
- 351.503(a)(1): proposed references "patterns of summary level in Sec. 430.208(d)" final "5 CFR 430.208(e)" — real cross-reference change (but maybe because 2026-13715 changed 430.208; still a difference).
- 351.503(b)(2): proposed "in accordance with Sec. 351.501"; final correction changes to "paragraph (a) of this section" (but that's correction 2026-17335; original final had Sec. 351.501). For Q11, compare proposed vs final as originally published or as corrected? Q11 says "regulatory text in the final rule (the amendments themselves...)". Probably final rule as corrected? Hmm. The final rule's original text at 351.503(b)(2) said "in accordance with Sec. 351.501 (as augmented..." then corrected to "paragraph (a) of this section." Q11 may expect the final rule as published/corrected. We should note corrections where relevant. But Q11 asks differences between proposed and final regulatory text. Could use final as corrected? We'll mention with correction note if a difference is affected.
- 351.503(d): proposed "(i.e., a pattern A 'pass/fail', or pattern D system)" final adds "authorized under 430.208(d) prior to the final rule prescribed at 91 FR 41521" (and corrected). Real addition.
- 351.503(e)(2): proposed no authorization clause; final adds (and corrected). Real addition.
- 351.504(a): proposed "should be identified"; final "must be identified." Real difference (mandatory vs should).
- 351.504(b): proposed "paragraph (b)(1), (2), or (3)" and "paragraph (b)(4) or (5)" final "paragraphs (b)(1), (2), or (3)" "paragraph (b)(4) or (b)(5)". Stylistic.
- 351.505(b)(2): proposed "covered by Sec. 351.503(b)" final "covered by Sec. 351.504(b)"—real cross-reference change (351.503 is performance, 351.504 is veterans preference). This is a significant correction in final.
- 351.505(c)(2): proposed "under paragraphs (a) and (b)" final "under paragraph (a) and paragraph (b)" stylistic.
- 351.506(c)(1): proposed "their performance credit ... and their service computation dates"; final "the employee's performance credit ... and the employee's service computation date." Hmm, final changes from plural to singular. Real? Could affect whose information is included; probably stylistic but maybe substantive. Q11 says real differences; this might count as wording only. Better focus on substantive.
- 351.506(c)(2): proposed cross-ref "Sec. 351.701(b) and (c)"; final original also (b) and (c), corrected to (b). Since final 351.701 no longer has (c) assignment rights (pay rates), correction fixes. Cross-reference change counts per Q11.
- 351.506(d): proposed "no right to review"; final adds "This paragraph does not limit any right of access available under another statute or regulation." Real addition.
- 351.507(a) same "receives" in both. Interesting: proposed 351.502 used "issues" but 351.507 used "receives"; final harmonized to "receives" in 351.502. Q5(c) asks event for tenure subgroup and retention standing: final uses receipt for both; proposed used issuance for tenure subgroup. Q11 difference.

Continue proposed 351.601 onward.

tools.name: fr_search

query.description: Full-text search terms; "" for none. Supports quoted phrases, e.g. "\"extension of stay\" F-1".

context.description: Lines of context around each match (default 2, at most 10).

tools.name: fr_text
tools.description: Read a document's full text by line range, with line numbers. [[Page N]] markers give FR page numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

answer.title: Answer

basis.description: Provisions and documents relied on, with citations.
basis.title: Basis

uncertainty.description: What the documents leave open, or "None".
uncertainty.title: Uncertainty

content.text:
More Q11 differences:
- 351.605: proposed structure as one paragraph (a) appropriate use, (b) abolishment with notice content embedded; final restructures into (a), (b), (c) Notice, (d) Retention register not required; final (c) adds "written notice in accordance with Sec. 351.801" and "must identify the competitive area being abolished"; final (d) says "must not apply assignment rights." Proposed (b) said "may not apply assignment rights" and embedded notice. Real structural/substantive differences.
- 351.606(a): proposed "When an agency applies Sec. 351.601, it shall give retention priorities over other competing employees to each competing employee entitled under Sec. 351.209(b)..." (note wrong cross-ref 351.209(b); final 353.209(b)) and final adds detailed paragraphs (a)(1)-(6): mandatory exception, reassignment, OPM placement, etc. Real major difference.
- 351.608(a)(2): proposed CTAP "part 330, subpart E"; final "subpart F". Real cross-reference change (Q11 says cross-reference to different section/subpart counts).
- 351.608(b): both 90 days. (g) 90 days.
- 351.701(b)(2): proposed "five grades ... (The agency uses ..." final same text mostly, with period/period placement. No.
- 351.701(a): final adds "or higher" after minimally satisfactory? Proposed: "minimally successful (Level 2) or equivalent, or higher"; final "minimally satisfactory (Level 2) or equivalent, or higher". Wording. Also final 351.701(b)(3) "pursuant to" vs proposed "pursuant the" typo.
- 351.702(a)(4)(iii): proposed "Does not solely include or principally rely on a self-assessment from an automated examination." Final "Does not consist solely of, or principally rely on, an automated self-assessment." Real wording; same meaning.
- Proposed 351.702(a)(4) lacks (v) exception for same position within 5 years with Level 3 rating. Final adds (v). Major real difference.
- 351.802: proposed revised (a)(2) and (3) only; final adds introductory text to (a) and same paragraphs with differences: proposed "veteran status" and "received during the last 4 years"; final "veterans' preference subgroup" and "received during the last 4 years"; proposed (a)(3) "A link to part 351 of this chapter and access to the agency's records"; final "A link to 5 CFR part 351 and information on how to access the agency's records". Real differences.
- 351.805: proposed did not amend; final adds 351.805(b) (amended notice solely later effective date not new notice; no recalculation). This is a significant real difference. But was it in proposed? Proposed rule TOC doesn't show 351.805. Final does. Yes.
- 351.807: final main RIF rule? TOC no; appeals rule amends 351.807(e). Not main rule.
- 351.202(d)(3)/(4): major final additions.
- 351.203 definitions: final adds "Restoration protected employee" and "Agency" maybe same; proposed did not add "Restoration protected employee" (list in proposed instruction 19 doesn't include; final includes). Real difference: final adds definition of "Restoration protected employee" in 351.203 (instruction 19(i)). Proposed had no such definition. This is a real difference and important for Q12 Farouk. Also final adds "modal rating" maybe not in instruction? Hmm, 351.503(f)(1) refers to "modal rating as defined in Sec. 351.203" in both proposed and final. Maybe "modal rating" already existed in 351.203 before; not added. Fine.

- 351.503(a)(1): proposed "Level 2 (Minimally Successful or equivalent)"; final "Level 2 (Minimally Satisfactory or equivalent)". Real? Could be considered wording, but "Minimally Successful" vs "Minimally Satisfactory" is a defined pattern term; likely real difference.
- 351.503(d): proposed "pattern A 'pass/fail', or pattern D system"; final adds parenthetical "authorized under 430.208(d) prior to the final rule prescribed at 91 FR 41521" (corrected). Real.
- 351.503(e)(2): same addition. Real.
- 351.503(f): proposed "and as follows"; final "and as follows" (same).
- 351.504(a): "should be identified" -> "must be identified". Real.
- 351.505(b)(2): "Sec. 351.503(b)" -> "Sec. 351.504(b)". Real.
- 351.506(d): final adds sentence. Real.
- 351.506(c)(2): cross-ref (b) and (c) -> final (b) (corrected). Real.
- 351.507: proposed and final same except proposed "under any of this paragraph (b)" vs final "under any of these provisions". Wording.
- 351.601(c): same? Proposed "identical performance credits as calculated pursuant to Sec. 351.503" same final.
- 351.602: same.
- 351.604: proposed amended 351.604(b) and removed (d); final main rule did NOT amend 351.604 (TOC shows "E. Part 351, Subpart F: Furloughs..." and section 2847 "Sec. 351.604 regarding furloughs of more than 30 consecutive calendar days..." Perhaps final decided not to finalize changes to RIF furlough procedures (summary item 6: "Not finalizing changes to RIF furlough procedures"). So proposed 351.604 changes were not finalized; that's a difference between proposed and final regulatory text: proposed would revise 351.604(b)/remove (d), final doesn't. This is a real difference (proposed text vs final text), and Q11 asks every real difference. We should include: proposed rule included amendments to 351.604; final rule did not adopt them (OPM elected not to finalize). But Q11 says "Compare the regulatory text of 5 CFR part 351 in the proposed rule with the regulatory text in the final rule (the amendments themselves...). List every real difference..." Yes, include non-adoption of 351.604 amendments. But maybe "the final rule's own summary of changes from proposal" mentions not finalizing changes to RIF furlough procedures. Still a real difference.
- 351.605 as above.
- 351.606 as above.
- 351.607 same.
- 351.608: proposed subpart E -> final subpart F cross-ref. Real.
- 351.701: final revised heading? Proposed instruction 34 "Revise heading for subpart G"; final instruction 33 "Revise Sec. 351.701" but TOC shows Subpart G Assignment Rights; maybe heading already changed? Actually final TOC line 5871 "Subpart G--Assignment Rights" without amendatory instruction? Proposed had instruction 34 revise heading. In final, there's no instruction to revise subpart G heading? The TOC line 5871 shows heading, but maybe from earlier? Hmm. In final text, instruction 33 revises 351.701; no instruction to revise heading. Could be already correct in CFR? Proposed proposed revise heading; final omitted. Not substantive.
- 351.702: final adds (v); real.
- 351.705: same.
- 351.802: as above.
- 351.805: final adds; real.

Also final 351.202(d)(4) notice requirement; final 351.203 definitions "Restoration protected employee"; final 351.402(c) OPM approval; final 351.204 merit principles; final 351.302(d) other procedures; final 351.502 receipt dates; final 351.505(b)(2) cross-ref; final 351.506(d); final 351.605 structure; final 351.606(a) detailed; final 351.702(a)(4)(v); final 351.805(b); final 351.503(d)/(e) authorization clauses; 351.504 mandatory "must"; 351.503(a)(1) 430.208(d)->(e); 351.203 "Rating of record" 430.208(d)->(e); 351.503(d)/(e) etc.

Also proposed 351.202(d)(2)(iii) "temporary or term appointment ... subpart C or D" vs final "temporary appointment ... subpart D"; 351.502(a)(3) same; 351.502(b)(3) etc. Also proposed 351.202(d)(1)(ii) trial period "as of the date the agency issues..." vs final "serving a trial period" (no date); (d)(2)(i)/(ii) proposed "as of the date the agency issues..." final no date. Real? Could be wording; the status is determined at RIF competition. We'll include the key ones.

Q11 asks "List every real difference between the two that you can find... Do not stop at the changes that the final rule's own summary of its changes from the proposal mentions." This is a demanding completeness question. We need be thorough but not list every stylistic difference. We should list differences of substance: changed scope, requirements, cross-references, added/removed provisions.

Need also check the final rule preamble "Summary of changes from proposed rule" mentions items 1-6: USERRA, merit principles, competitive area safeguards, clarifying exclusions 351.202(d), various clarifying changes (351.605, 351.203/359.802, 353.110, 351.802(a), 351.805, 362.306), not finalizing 351.604. So Q11 wants additional differences beyond those summary items. Many are in final but not mentioned: e.g., 351.502 "receives" vs "issues"; 351.503(a)(1) reference to 430.208(e); 351.504 "must" vs "should"; 351.505(b)(2) cross-ref; 351.506(c)(2) cross-ref and (d) sentence; 351.606(a) detail (maybe USERRA summary mentions mandatory exception but not all detail); 351.607? 351.608 subpart F; 351.702(a)(4)(v) maybe summary item 13 mentions exception for same position (executive summary, not final summary of changes from proposal); 351.802(a)(2) veteran status -> veterans' preference subgroup (preamble section says OPM changed from proposed; that's mentioned in section-by-section but not summary of changes). Q11 says don't stop at changes the final rule's own summary mentions. We can include all.

But "every real difference" is almost impossible; need reasonable comprehensive list with paragraph-level accuracy. We'll compile later.

Now Q13: preamble vs regulatory text of main final rule. Need read section-by-section analysis and compare. Let's read the main final rule's section-by-section for subparts B-E, F, G, H. Lines 1539-3198. That's 1660 lines ~25k tokens. We have ~72k tokens left. We can afford maybe 40k more reading plus writing. Need also read Q9 provisions in preamble maybe not necessary; regulatory text enough.

Let's read 1539-2100 (Subpart B and C, D) first.

cfr.description: CFR title:part affected, e.g. 8:214. The part must be numeric; lettered parts are not supported by this filter.

tools.description: Search U.S. Federal Register documents (rules, proposed rules, notices, presidential documents) by keywords and filters. Prints document numbers, titles, types, dates, citations, dockets, RINs and abstracts.

tools.name: fr_doc
tools.description: Metadata for one Federal Register document: title, type, action, citation, page range, publication/signing/effective dates, comment deadline, docket, RIN, CFR parts affected, corrections, abstract.

tools.name: fr_toc
tools.description: Outline of a document's full text: headings with line numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_grep

pattern.description: Python regular expression, searched over the whole text (a match may span lines). ^ and $ match at line boundaries; . does not match a newline.
pattern.title: Pattern

context.description: Lines of context around each match (default 2, at most 10).
context.title: Context

tools.description: Regex search inside one document's full text. Shows the lines of each match with line numbers, context lines and the FR page of each match. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_text
tools.description: Read a document's full text by line range, with line numbers. [[Page N]] markers give FR page numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

basis.description: Provisions and documents relied on, with citations.

[2026-15665: lines 1539-1938 of 6220, FR page 49190]
  1539  III. Section-by-Section Analysis and Response to Comments
  1540  
  1541      OPM responds to comments regarding specific sections of this rule 
  1542  below.
  1543  
  1544  A. Part 351, Subpart B: Changes in Definitions, Coverage, Use of 
  1545  Regulations, and Agency Responsibilities
  1546  
  1547  1. Erosion of Duties Reclassifications
  1548      OPM is modifying Sec.  351.201(a)(2) to remove from the list of 
  1549  actions that require agencies to use RIF procedures reclassification of 
  1550  an employee's position due to erosion of duties if the action would 
  1551  take effect after an agency had formally announced a RIF in the 
  1552  employee's competitive area and the RIF would take effect within 180 
  1553  days.
  1554      Commenter 0532 argued that OPM has not justified removing erosion-
  1555  of-duties reclassifications from the actions requiring RIF procedures. 
  1556  OPM disagrees.
  1557      The proposed rule explains the history of the erosion-of-duties 
  1558  provision. In 1986, OPM generally removed erosion-of-duties 
  1559  reclassifications from the categories of actions subject to RIF 
  1560  procedures, but retained a narrow RIF-procedure requirement for 
  1561  reclassifications occurring after announcement of a RIF and within 180 
  1562  days of the RIF effective date. OPM is now removing that narrow 
  1563  procedural trigger because it is unreasonable and impracticable to 
  1564  require agencies to build a retention register for such 
  1565  reclassifications, and OPM is not aware of any agency actually 
  1566  executing an erosion-of-duties reclassification action using RIF 
  1567  procedures since the 1986 revision.
  1568      Commenter 0037 argued that the ``erosion of duties'' changes could 
  1569  be used to constructively demote disfavored employees. OPM disagrees. 
  1570  Erosion of duties reclassifications have generally been excluded from 
  1571  RIF procedures since 1986, except in the narrow circumstance where the 
  1572  reclassification will take effect after an agency has formally 
  1573  announced a RIF in the employee's competitive area that will take 
  1574  effect within 180 days. This rule directly addresses concerns that 
  1575  erosion-of-duties reclassifications could be used to undermine the RIF 
  1576  retention order. Rather than requiring a full RIF process for erosion-
  1577  of-duties reclassifications, this rule will bar agencies from 
  1578  undertaking an erosion-of-duties reclassification between the formal 
  1579  announcement and completion of a RIF if the action would adversely 
  1580  affect an employee's retention standing in the RIF. This is a more 
  1581  direct and administrable safeguard than the current rule. Notably, 
  1582  commenters 0037 and 0532 do not identify any concrete instance in which 
  1583  the existing erosion-of-duties RIF trigger has been necessary to 
  1584  protect employees, nor do
  1585  
  1586  [[Page 49191]]
  1587  
  1588  commenters 0037 or 0532 explain why the proposed anti-manipulation 
  1589  prohibition would be inadequate.
  1590      Instead, OPM agrees with Commenter 0720, a Federal agency, that the 
  1591  current erosion-of-duties provision is outdated, and OPM's approach in 
  1592  this rule ``reduces unnecessary confusion and risk while preserving 
  1593  safeguards against improper alterations to retention outcomes.''
  1594  2. Employees Excluded From RIF Competition
  1595      This rule modifies the definition of the term Competing employee in 
  1596  Sec.  351.203 to mean an employee in the competitive service tenure 
  1597  group or the excepted service tenure group. It also adds a definition 
  1598  of Competitive service tenure group to mean all employees within 
  1599  competitive service tenure subgroups I and II; that is, all employees 
  1600  in the competitive service who, as of the date of the RIF notice, are 
  1601  not serving an initial probationary period or a temporary appointment 
  1602  of 1 year or less under subpart D of 5 CFR part 316. This rule defines 
  1603  the Excepted service tenure group as all employees within excepted 
  1604  service tenure subgroups I and II; that is, all excepted service 
  1605  appointees serving in a career position (that is, not in Schedule C or 
  1606  G) who, as of the date of the RIF notice, are not serving a trial 
  1607  period or in a temporary or time-limited appointment of 1 year or less.
  1608      OPM is also adding definitions of initial probationary period and 
  1609  trial period to Sec.  351.203. With respect to these provisions, OPM 
  1610  notes that a supervisory or managerial employee with career tenure who 
  1611  is only on probation with respect to those supervisory or managerial 
  1612  functions (i.e., is entitled to be returned to a nonsupervisory or non-
  1613  managerial position rather than being subject to removal under 5 CFR 
  1614  part 315, subpart I) would be included in the RIF in the supervisory or 
  1615  managerial position, and would not be subject to the exclusion from RIF 
  1616  procedures applicable to individuals serving an initial probationary 
  1617  period under 5 CFR 11.2. Further, an employee who is serving both an 
  1618  initial probationary period and a supervisory probationary period 
  1619  simultaneously is exempt from RIF procedures.
  1620      In the proposed rule, OPM proposed to add a Sec.  351.202(d) that 
  1621  lists categories of employees excluded from RIF retention procedures, 
  1622  as they fall outside the definition of ``competing employees'' under 5 
  1623  U.S.C. 3502(a). Under OPM's definition of ``competing employees,'' 
  1624  employees in the competitive service who are serving an initial 
  1625  probationary period would be excluded from RIF procedures, as would 
  1626  employees in the excepted service who are serving a trial period. In 
  1627  addition, competitive and excepted service employees who are serving 
  1628  temporary or time-limited appointments of 1 year or less would be 
  1629  excluded from RIF competition, as would Schedule C and Schedule G 
  1630  employees.
  1631      In this final rule, OPM is revising the wording of Sec.  
  1632  351.202(d). The revised wording narrows Sec.  351.202(d) from a broad 
  1633  statement that certain employees are excluded from part 351 altogether 
  1634  to a more precise statement that they are not ``competing employees'' 
  1635  for RIF purposes. The final rule clarifies the consequences of this 
  1636  classification: an agency may retain such an employee while releasing a 
  1637  competing employee, and may furlough, separate, demote, or reassign 
  1638  such an employee for a reason described in Sec.  351.201(a)(2) (lack of 
  1639  work, shortage of funds, insufficient personnel ceiling, 
  1640  reorganization, or the exercise of reemployment rights or restoration 
  1641  rights) without determining the employee's retention standing under 
  1642  subparts D and E, applying the order-of-release provisions in subpart 
  1643  F, or providing assignment rights under subpart G, provided the action 
  1644  is otherwise consistent with the terms of the employee's appointment 
  1645  and applicable law. Further, the revised text clarifies that these 
  1646  excluded employees are still subject to the notice provisions of Sec.  
  1647  351.801 where they are furloughed for more than 30 days, separated, 
  1648  demoted, or reassigned for the reasons described in Sec.  
  1649  351.201(a)(2), and the action is not merely the expiration of a 
  1650  temporary or time-limited appointment according to its terms. Under 
  1651  such circumstances the agency must provide the employee a modified 
  1652  written notice that includes the action to be taken, the reasons for 
  1653  the action, and its effective date; a link to 5 CFR part 351 and access 
  1654  to the agency's records pertinent to the reduction in force being 
  1655  taken; information on reemployment rights; and any appeal rights.
  1656      In addition, the final rule makes other wording changes to Sec.  
  1657  351.202(d). It revises the Schedule C and Schedule G language by 
  1658  referring to employees ``serving under'' those appointments and removes 
  1659  a proposed reference to term appointments under part 316 subpart C, 
  1660  making clear that the competitive-service temporary-appointment 
  1661  exclusion is limited to temporary appointments of 1 year or less under 
  1662  part 316 subpart D.
  1663      Commenter 0719, a Federal agency, supported the proposed changes 
  1664  excluding initial probationary period and trial period employees from 
  1665  RIF competition, noting that the current RIF rules demand that 
  1666  probationary and trial period employees be released first in a RIF. 
  1667  Commenter 0719 noted that this results in ``the loss of high potential 
  1668  individuals essential for long term succession planning and mission 
  1669  continuity.'' The agency noted that ``[r]emoving these groups from RIF 
  1670  competition will allow [it] greater flexibility to retain high 
  1671  potential early career employees even in constrained budget 
  1672  conditions.'' Commenter 0687 noted that termination of probationary 
  1673  employees as part of workforce reshaping activities can ``weaken[] 
  1674  early career pipelines'' and result in the loss of some of the agency's 
  1675  ``best talent.'' OPM agrees.
  1676      Commenter 0678 claimed that these exclusions would mean that the 
  1677  RIF regulations would no longer provide a comprehensive system to 
  1678  govern workforce reductions, while Commenter 0684 argued that this 
  1679  change would conflict with 5 U.S.C. 3501(b)'s broad coverage provision. 
  1680  OPM disagrees. OPM has long used its authority under 5 U.S.C. 3502 to 
  1681  define the otherwise-undefined statutory term ``competing employees'' 
  1682  subject to RIF competition to exclude certain groups of employees from 
  1683  RIF retention procedures. For example, in its regulations at 5 CFR 
  1684  316.911, OPM recognizes that employees ``whose initial appointment [is] 
  1685  for a period of 1 year or less are not assigned a tenure group and do 
  1686  not compete with other employees in a RIF.'' In its regulations at 5 
  1687  CFR 353.209, OPM stated that an employee performing duty with the 
  1688  uniformed services ``is not a `competing employee' under'' the RIF 
  1689  regulations. And OPM's regulations at 5 CFR 351.705 have long provided 
  1690  that an agency may, but is not required to, provide assignment rights 
  1691  to excepted service employees.
  1692      Related statutory provisions, and the broader history of 
  1693  probationary and trial periods in the Federal service, support OPM's 
  1694  determination that probationary and trial period employees should not 
  1695  be considered ``competing employees'' for purposes of 5 U.S.C. 3502. 
  1696  The phrase ``competing employee'' in 5 U.S.C. 3502 must be read against 
  1697  a long background tracing to the Pendleton Act of 1883 whereby Congress 
  1698  has consistently and deliberately maintained a distinction between 
  1699  employees whose appointments have become final and employees still 
  1700  serving a probationary or trial period. This distinction reflects a 
  1701  longstanding congressional and regulatory judgment that competitive 
  1702  selection alone is not the final test of fitness for Federal
  1703  
  1704  [[Page 49192]]
  1705  
  1706  service. Rather, an initial period of actual service has always served 
  1707  as the Government's final opportunity to determine whether an employee 
  1708  should receive the full procedural protections associated with 
  1709  continuing Federal employment.
  1710      The Pendleton Act (22 Stat. 403) required that the ``there shall be 
  1711  a period of probation before any absolute appointment or employment 
  1712  aforesaid.'' That statutory formulation indicates that Congress did not 
  1713  treat appointment and final appointment as the same event. It preserved 
  1714  a two-step process--competitive appointment first, with final 
  1715  appointment only after satisfactory completion of probation.
  1716      In its first annual report in 1884, the Civil Service Commission 
  1717  characterized the probationary period as lasting ``six months before 
  1718  any absolute appointment can be made. At the end of this time the 
  1719  appointee goes out of the service unless then reappointed.'' \7\ Two 
  1720  years later, the Commission wrote in its third annual report that 
  1721  ``doing the public work is precisely what the Merit System provides. If 
  1722  at its termination the appointing officer is not . . . willing to make 
  1723  an unconditional appointment, the probationer is . . . absolutely out 
  1724  of the service without any action on the part of the Government.'' \8\
  1725  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1726  
  1727      \7\ First Annual Report of the United States Civil Service 
  1728  Commission to the President (1884), p. 29, https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=nnc1.cu09006737&seq=9.
  1729      \8\ Third Annual Report of the United States Civil Service 
  1730  Commission to the President (1886), p. 36, https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=njp.32101073361022&seq=40.
  1731  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1732  
  1733      With the enactment of the Lloyd-La Follette Act of 1912, Congress 
  1734  created the first legislative codification of protection against 
  1735  removal for civil servants. The Act established ``[t]hat no person in 
  1736  the classified civil service of the United States shall be removed 
  1737  therefrom except for such cause as will promote the efficiency of said 
  1738  service.'' \9\ The Act also imposed certain procedural requirements on 
  1739  removals including advance notice and an opportunity to respond in 
  1740  writing. However, Congress did not establish employment protections for 
  1741  probationary employees, and has maintained this exclusion through every 
  1742  subsequent recodification of the civil service laws.
  1743  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1744  
  1745      \9\ The Lloyd-La Follette Act, 37 Stat. 555 (1912), as amended, 
  1746  62 Stat. 354 (1948), 5 U.S.C.A. 652(a).
  1747  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1748  
  1749      Congress legislated against this backdrop in using the term 
  1750  ``competing employees'' in the Veterans' Preference Act of 1944 \10\--
  1751  the direct legislative predecessor of 5 U.S.C. 3502. The Veterans' 
  1752  Preference Act of 1944 did not define ``competing employees'' to 
  1753  include all individuals serving in Federal positions. Instead, Section 
  1754  12 of that Act provided that, in a reduction in personnel, ``competing 
  1755  employees'' would be released in accordance with Civil Service 
  1756  Commission regulations giving due effect to the statutory retention 
  1757  factors. Congress thus left the identification of the competitive group 
  1758  to regulation.
  1759  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1760  
  1761      \10\ Public Law 78-359, 58 Stat. 387 (codified, as amended in 
  1762  part, at 5 U.S.C. 3309-3320).
  1763  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1764  
  1765      This is particularly significant because, in Section 14, the 
  1766  Veterans' Preference Act expanded civil service protections to 
  1767  preference eligible Federal employees, but it explicitly excluded 
  1768  probationers, limiting its protections to a ``permanent or indefinite 
  1769  preference eligible, who has completed a probationary or trial 
  1770  period.'' Section 12 and section 14 were enacted in the same statute. 
  1771  If Congress believed probationary and trial-period employees 
  1772  necessarily had to be treated the same as final appointees for all 
  1773  retention-related purposes, it would be odd for Congress, two sections 
  1774  later, to condition major procedural protections on completion of 
  1775  probationary or trial service. The better reading is that the 1944 Act 
  1776  preserved a two-step civil-service model: an employee could enter 
  1777  Federal service and receive whatever preference rights the statute and 
  1778  regulations afforded, but the employee did not necessarily become part 
  1779  of the competitive retention workforce before completing the 
  1780  probationary or trial period.
  1781      The statutory text of 5 U.S.C. 3502(a) therefore does not compel 
  1782  OPM to include employees serving an initial probationary or trial 
  1783  period in RIF competition; rather, it permits OPM to determine by 
  1784  regulation that such employees are not ``competing employees'' for 
  1785  purposes of retention registers and order of release, while preserving 
  1786  any independently applicable statutory or regulatory protections.\11\
  1787  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1788  
  1789      \11\ Commenter 0684 points to Fathauer v. United States, 566 
  1790  F.3d 1352 (Fed. Cir. 2009), but that case is inapposite. Here, OPM 
  1791  is not defining ``employee'' in 5 U.S.C. 3501(b) to nullify 
  1792  statutory coverage. Instead, it is defining the narrower, undefined 
  1793  term ``competing employee'' in section 3502(a), a term Congress 
  1794  expressly left for implementation through OPM regulations.
  1795  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1796  
  1797      The current 5 U.S.C. 7511 codifies the longstanding exclusion of 
  1798  probationary and trial period employees from the adverse-action 
  1799  definition of ``employee.'' Under 5 U.S.C. 7511, an ``employee'' in the 
  1800  competitive service or excepted service generally means an individual 
  1801  who is not serving a probationary or trial period under an initial 
  1802  appointment or who has completed one year of current continuous service 
  1803  under other than a temporary appointment limited to one year or less.
  1804      Courts interpreting section 7511 and related CSRA provisions have 
  1805  repeatedly recognized that Congress intended agencies to retain 
  1806  substantial flexibility over probationary and trial-period employees. 
  1807  In Department of Justice v. FLRA, the D.C. Circuit relied on the CSRA's 
  1808  structure and legislative history in concluding that probationary 
  1809  employees could not obtain through negotiated grievance procedures the 
  1810  kind of review Congress deliberately withheld from them in chapter 
  1811  75.\12\ 709 F.2d 724, 730 (D.C. Cir. 1983). In United States v. 
  1812  Connolly, the Federal Circuit likewise treated the exclusion of 
  1813  probationary employees from chapter 75 appeal rights as a deliberate 
  1814  congressional choice, not a statutory gap for courts or agencies to 
  1815  fill.\13\ And in National Treasury Employees Union v. FLRA, the D.C. 
  1816  Circuit reaffirmed that the CSRA's treatment of probationary employees 
  1817  reflects Congress's judgment that agencies must have latitude to assess 
  1818  and separate employees who have not yet completed the testing period 
  1819  for Federal service.\14\ This history does not mean that section 7511 
  1820  directly controls chapter 35 RIF procedures. It does, however, confirm 
  1821  that OPM's treatment of probationary, trial-period, and short-term 
  1822  temporary employees in this rule is consistent with the broader civil-
  1823  service framework Congress enacted.
  1824  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1825  
  1826      \12\ See Dep't of Justice v. FLRA, 709 F.2d 724, 730 (D.C. Cir. 
  1827  1983).
  1828      \13\ See U.S. v. Connolly, 716 F.2d 882, 886 (Fed. Cir. 1983).
  1829      \14\ See Nat'l Treasury Emps. Union v. FLRA, 848 F.2d 1273, 1275 
  1830  (D.C. Cir. 1988).
  1831  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1832  
  1833      In addition, 5 U.S.C. 3502 should be read consistent with 5 U.S.C. 
  1834  3321, which contemplates a probationary period before an appointment 
  1835  becomes final and allows the President to issue rules and regulations 
  1836  effectuating probationary periods. Current Civil Service Rule 11, 
  1837  issued by the President under Executive Order (E.O.) 14284, already 
  1838  supplies a comprehensive framework for probationary and trial-period 
  1839  employment. It requires agencies to use probationary and trial periods 
  1840  to evaluate whether an employee's continuation in Federal service 
  1841  advances the public interest and expressly permits agencies to consider 
  1842  agency needs and interests, whether continued employment would advance 
  1843  agency or Government organizational goals, and whether continued
  1844  
  1845  [[Page 49193]]
  1846  
  1847  employment would advance the efficiency of the service.
  1848      Those considerations substantially overlap with the reasons 
  1849  agencies conduct RIFs, including lack of work, shortage of funds, and 
  1850  reorganization. Requiring agencies to apply full part 351 retention-
  1851  register, order-of-release, and assignment-right procedures to 
  1852  employees whose appointments have not yet become final would duplicate 
  1853  Rule 11 and could produce inconsistent outcomes. For example, Rule 11 
  1854  might support retaining a probationary employee because the employee 
  1855  has scarce skills, strong actual performance, and is needed for the 
  1856  agency's future mission. But a part 351 retention register would likely 
  1857  place the same employee low because the employee has little service 
  1858  time and may lack a rating of record. Thus, excluding probationary and 
  1859  trial period employees from the statutory definition of ``competing 
  1860  employees'' in 5 U.S.C. 3502(a) eliminates duplication and makes sense 
  1861  of the overall statutory scheme.
  1862      With respect to temporary employees, OPM's regulations at 5 CFR 
  1863  part 316, subpart D make clear that such appointments are only 
  1864  appropriate to meet short-term needs, including ``for such reasons as 
  1865  abolishment, reorganization, or contracting of the function, 
  1866  anticipated reduction in funding, or completion of a specific project 
  1867  or peak workload.'' 5 CFR 316.401(a)(2). Further, ``[t]he supervisor of 
  1868  each position filled by temporary appointment must certify that the 
  1869  employment need is truly temporary and that the proposed appointment 
  1870  meets the regulatory time limits.'' Id. 316.401(b). Thus, these 
  1871  regulations indicate that temporary employees do not have a reasonable 
  1872  expectation of long-term employment and thus should not be considered 
  1873  ``competing employees'' for purposes of 5 U.S.C. 3502.
  1874      Further, in the final rule, OPM has clarified that the employees 
  1875  excluded from RIF competition are not entirely outside the regulatory 
  1876  scheme and must receive a notice in accordance with 5 U.S.C. 3502(d) 
  1877  when they are furloughed for more than 30 days, separated, demoted, or 
  1878  reassigned for reasons of lack of work, shortage of funds, insufficient 
  1879  personnel ceiling, reorganization, or the exercise of reemployment 
  1880  rights or restoration rights and the action is not merely the 
  1881  expiration of a temporary or time-limited appointment according to its 
  1882  terms. In addition, the regulations provide in Sec.  351.605 that all 
  1883  positions in the competitive area, including those of employees 
  1884  excluded from RIF competition under Sec.  351.202(d), must be abolished 
  1885  within 180 days for an agency to permissibly use the streamlined 
  1886  procedures of that subpart.
  1887      Commenter 0672 objected that probationary employees can be covered 
  1888  by the proposal's missing-rating rules and therefore should remain in 
  1889  RIF competition. OPM does not agree that the proposed modal-rating 
  1890  provision eliminates the need to exclude probationary and trial-period 
  1891  employees from RIF competition. The modal-rating rule is a limited 
  1892  proxy for competing employees who lack ratings in the applicable 
  1893  lookback period; it does not provide an individualized measure of 
  1894  performance for employees whose appointments have not yet been 
  1895  finalized and who often have not served long enough to receive a rating 
  1896  of record. In a performance-first RIF system, assigning retention 
  1897  standing to such employees based on the most common rating assigned to 
  1898  other employees would fail to measure the employee's own performance. 
  1899  OPM therefore reasonably treats probationary and trial-period employees 
  1900  outside the retention-register process and permits agencies to retain, 
  1901  finalize, or separate them under the rules applicable to their 
  1902  appointments, instead of the RIF rules.
  1903      Further, the modal-rating approach does not address the separate 
  1904  legal and personnel-management function of probationary and trial 
  1905  periods. Civil Service Rule 11 provides that agencies must use 
  1906  probationary and trial periods to evaluate an employee's fitness and 
  1907  whether continued employment advances the public interest; the agency 
  1908  may consider performance and conduct, agency needs, organizational 
  1909  goals, and efficiency of the service before finalizing the appointment. 
  1910  A modal RIF rating cannot replace that appointment-finalization 
  1911  judgment. It does not tell the agency whether the employee has 
  1912  demonstrated sufficient fitness, adaptability, conduct, judgment, or 
  1913  mission fit to warrant final appointment. It simply imputes a rating 
  1914  based on how other employees were rated. That is a poor fit for 
  1915  employees who are still in the government's final assessment period.
  1916      Commenters 0674 and 0680 argued that excluding temporary, 
  1917  probationary and trial period employees from RIF procedures could mean 
  1918  that certain employees still covered by RIF regulations would be 
  1919  released ahead of more junior employees, thus undermining tenure as a 
  1920  statutory retention factor. But 5 U.S.C. 3502 does not prescribe a 
  1921  strict ``last in, first out'' system. It does not define ``competing 
  1922  employees,'' does not require every employee in an agency to compete 
  1923  against every other employee, and does not require agencies to retain 
  1924  every more senior employee ahead of every less senior employee in all 
  1925  circumstances. Instead, it directed OPM to create regulations for the 
  1926  release of competing employees and to give ``due effect'' to several 
  1927  factors. ``Due effect'' does not mean controlling effect, equal effect, 
  1928  or absolute effect in every possible comparison. Nor does it mean that 
  1929  tenure must always override appointment status, performance, agency 
  1930  needs, or the threshold question whether an employee has a finalized 
  1931  appointment and belongs in RIF competition at all. OPM therefore may 
  1932  reasonably distinguish between employees who have completed the period 
  1933  necessary to obtain a finalized appointment and employees who remain in 
  1934  a temporary, probationary, or trial status.
  1935      Commenter 0115 expressed concern that excluding probationary and 
  1936  temporary employees from RIF procedures might hurt efforts to recruit 
  1937  early-career talent. However, probationary, trial period, and temporary 
  1938  employees are the most likely to be separated under the current RIF

Interesting Q13 candidate: At lines 1548-1553, preamble says OPM is modifying Sec. 351.201(a)(2) "to remove from the list of actions that require agencies to use RIF procedures reclassification of an employee's position due to erosion of duties if the action would take effect after an agency had formally announced a RIF ... and the RIF would take effect within 180 days." But the regulatory text amends 351.202(c)(3), not 351.201(a)(2). The amendatory instruction 17 revises 351.201(a)(2) but that's the list of RIF actions; the erosion-of-duties provision is in 351.202(c)(3) (instruction 18). So preamble says modifying Sec. 351.201(a)(2) when actual amendment is to 351.202(c)(3). Also substantive: preamble says remove erosion-of-duties reclassification from actions requiring RIF procedures "if the action would take effect after an agency had formally announced a RIF ... and the RIF would take effect within 180 days"; but regulatory text 351.202(c)(3) says "except that an agency shall not undertake such a reclassification action between the time an agency has formally announced a reduction in force in the employee's competitive area and the completion of the reduction in force where the reclassification action would adversely affect an employee's retention standing." No 180-day condition; the trigger is adverse effect on retention standing, and period ends at completion. This is a strong Q13 item: preamble describing 351.201(a)(2) vs actual 351.202(c)(3), plus different trigger (180 days vs adverse effect). Does another preamble passage state correctly? Later at lines 1574-1581: "this rule will bar agencies from undertaking an erosion-of-duties reclassification between the formal announcement and completion of a RIF if the action would adversely affect an employee's retention standing." That's correct. Also lines 1557-1562 describe "current" 180-day rule, not this rule. So Q13 item #1: preamble at 91 FR 49190 says modifying 351.201(a)(2) and describes 180-day trigger; regulatory text at 91 FR 49218 amends 351.202(c)(3) with adverse-effect trigger; another passage (91 FR 49191) states correct.

Also lines 1600-1607: "as of the date of the RIF notice" vs text 351.502 "as of the date the employee receives a specific reduction in force notice." Preamble says "date of the RIF notice" ambiguous; could be issuance vs receipt. Since final changed to receipt, preamble "date of the RIF notice" may be inaccurate. Q13 candidate: preamble at 49191 refers to "as of the date of the RIF notice," while text uses "date the employee receives a specific reduction in force notice." Does another passage state correctly? Maybe later lines 2284 etc. say "date the employee receives a specific reduction in force notice." Need note.

Also lines 1617-1619: "an employee who is serving both an initial probationary period and a supervisory probationary period simultaneously is exempt from RIF procedures." Wait, regulatory text 351.202(d) excludes employees serving an initial probationary period; a supervisory probationary period alone is not an initial probationary period (351.203 definition excludes supervisory probation). If an employee is serving both, yes initial probationary excludes. Fine.

Lines 1620-1630: "competitive and excepted service employees who are serving temporary or time-limited appointments of 1 year or less would be excluded." But final text 351.202(d)(2)(iii) excludes only temporary appointments ≤1 year under subpart D; not term appointments under subpart C; and 351.502(a)(3) subgroup II excludes "temporary appointment of 1 year or less under subpart D". So preamble broad statement "temporary or time-limited appointments of 1 year or less" could be inaccurate for competitive service term appointments (e.g., 351.202(d)(2)(iii) doesn't exclude term appointments). But it says "competitive and excepted service employees" — in excepted service (d)(1)(i) includes temporary or time-limited; in competitive service only temporary. Q13 candidate: preamble at 49191 says competitive and excepted employees serving temporary or time-limited appointments ≤1 year excluded; regulatory text at 49218 limits competitive-service exclusion to temporary appointments of one year or less under part 316 subpart D, not time-limited/term. Does another passage state correctly? Lines 1656-1662 correct: "removes a proposed reference to term appointments under part 316 subpart C, making clear that the competitive-service temporary-appointment exclusion is limited to temporary appointments of 1 year or less under part 316 subpart D." So another passage states correctly. Strong Q13 item.

Lines 1650-1655: describes modified notice content "includes the action to be taken, the reasons for the action, and its effective date; a link to 5 CFR part 351 and access to agency records; information on reemployment rights; and any appeal rights." But 351.202(d)(4) says notice "must include notification content in accordance with Sec. 351.802(a)(1), (a)(3), (a)(5), (a)(6) and (b)" and "must state that the employee is not a competing employee ... and therefore was not ranked..." It excludes (a)(2) and (a)(4). What are (a)(1), (a)(3), (a)(5), (a)(6), (b)? We don't have them printed. Preamble summary may be inaccurate? Hard to say. Could be a Q13 candidate if preamble says notice includes information on reemployment rights (a)(5) and appeal rights (a)(6), consistent. Fine.

Now Subpart D preamble (competitive areas) lines 2137-2253. Read.
